cpu.temp.nodriver.title: CPU temperature could not be read
cpu.temp.nodriver.detail: Reading CPU sensors requires the PawnIO driver, which does not seem to be installed.
cpu.temp.nodriver.fix: Install PawnIO (pawnio.eu) and restart CHC to see CPU temperature, clocks and power.
cpu.temp.needadmin.title: CPU temperature is not available in limited mode
cpu.temp.needadmin.detail: Windows only allows CPU sensors to be read with administrator rights.
cpu.temp.needadmin.fix: Restart CHC as administrator. If it still cannot be read, install the PawnIO driver (pawnio.eu).
cpu.temp.critical.title: The processor is overheating ({0:0} °C)
cpu.temp.critical.detail: Above 100 °C the processor slows itself down and the computer may crash or shut off.
cpu.temp.critical.fix: Make sure the CPU cooler fan spins, remove dust and renew the thermal paste if the computer is a few years old.
cpu.temp.highidle.title: The processor runs hot at low load ({0:0} °C at {1:0}% load)
cpu.temp.highidle.detail: A processor this warm while mostly idle usually points to a cooling problem.
cpu.temp.highidle.fix: Clean the cooler and case fans, check that the cooler is mounted firmly and that nothing blocks the airflow.
cpu.temp.high.title: Processor temperature is high ({0:0} °C at {1:0}% load)
cpu.temp.high.detail: Some modern processors run up to 90–95 °C under heavy load by design, but sustained high temperatures shorten component life.
cpu.temp.high.fix: Improve case airflow or consider a stronger cooler if this happens often.
cpu.temp.ok.title: Processor temperature is normal ({0:0} °C)
cpu.load.high.title: The processor was very busy during the scan ({0:0}%)
cpu.load.high.detail: Something was using most of the processor while CHC was scanning.
cpu.load.high.fix: Open Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc) to see which program is using the CPU.
cpu.virtualization.off.title: Hardware virtualization is turned off
cpu.virtualization.off.detail: WSL2, Hyper-V, Android emulators and some Windows security features need it.
cpu.virtualization.off.fix: If you need these features, enable SVM (AMD) or VT-x (Intel) in the BIOS/UEFI settings.
cpu.ok.title: No processor problems detected
cpu.temp.peak.title: The processor reached {0:0} °C while CHC was open
cpu.temp.peak.detail: The processor cools down quickly after a game, so the peak matters more than the current value.
cpu.temp.peak.fix: Clean the cooler and fans, check the cooler mounting and improve case airflow.
cpu.ryzen.idle.title: Some AMD Ryzen systems freeze when idle
cpu.ryzen.idle.detail: A deep power-saving state can make some Ryzen PCs freeze at very low load, for example when left alone.
cpu.ryzen.idle.fix: Update the BIOS. In the BIOS, set "Power Supply Idle Control" to "Typical Current Idle" if it exists.
cpu.smt.off.title: Simultaneous multithreading (SMT) is off
cpu.smt.off.detail: This {0}-core processor can run two threads per core, but only {0} threads are active. Modern games and multitasking usually run better with SMT on.
cpu.smt.off.fix: Turn SMT back on in the BIOS (usually Advanced → AMD CBS → CPU Common Options → SMT Control → Auto).
memory.load.high.title: Memory is almost full ({0:0}% in use)
memory.load.high.detail: When RAM runs out, Windows moves data to the disk and everything slows down.
memory.load.high.fix: Close programs you don't need, check Task Manager for memory-hungry apps or consider adding more RAM.
memory.load.elevated.title: Memory usage is high ({0:0}%)
memory.load.elevated.detail: There is still free memory, but not much headroom for demanding tasks.
memory.load.ok.title: Memory usage is normal ({0:0}%)
memory.commit.high.title: Virtual memory is nearly exhausted ({0:0}%)
memory.commit.high.detail: Programs may crash with "out of memory" errors.
memory.commit.high.fix: Close some programs or let Windows manage the page file size.
memory.capacity.low.title: Low memory capacity ({0})
memory.capacity.low.detail: 8 GB or more is recommended for Windows 11 and modern apps.
memory.capacity.low.fix: Adding RAM is one of the cheapest upgrades for a noticeably faster computer.
memory.singlechannel.title: Memory runs in single-channel mode
memory.singlechannel.detail: Only one memory module is installed although the board has {0} slots. Dual-channel memory gives much more bandwidth, especially for games and integrated graphics.
memory.singlechannel.fix: Add a second identical module to enable dual-channel mode.
memory.speed.below.title: Memory runs below its rated speed ({0} of {1} MT/s)
memory.speed.below.detail: The modules support a higher speed than they are currently running at.
memory.speed.below.fix: Enable XMP / EXPO in the BIOS to run the memory at its rated speed.
memory.mixed.title: Different memory modules are mixed
memory.mixed.detail: Modules with different sizes or models can limit speed or stability.
memory.mixed.fix: For the best results use identical modules (a matched kit).
memory.lowmemory.title: Critical low-memory events in the last {1} days: {0}
memory.lowmemory.detail: When memory runs out, programs freeze or are closed by Windows.
memory.lowmemory.fix: Look for a program that keeps using more memory (a memory leak), close programs, or add RAM.
memory.test.errors.title: Windows Memory Diagnostic found errors ({0})
memory.test.errors.detail: A memory module or its settings are faulty.
memory.test.errors.fix: Turn off XMP/EXPO and test again. If errors remain, test the modules one by one and replace the faulty one.
memory.test.suggest.title: Test the memory
memory.test.suggest.detail: Freezes and crashes are often caused by memory errors, and this PC's memory has not been tested in the last year.
memory.test.suggest.fix: Run "Windows Memory Diagnostic" from the Start menu (the PC restarts for the test).
memory.xmp.stability.title: Memory runs an overclocked XMP/EXPO profile ({0} MT/s)
memory.xmp.stability.detail: XMP/EXPO is a factory overclock. It works on most PCs, but it is one of the most common causes of crashes and freezes.
memory.xmp.stability.fix: To test, turn XMP/EXPO off in the BIOS for a few days. If the problems stop, use a slightly lower speed or update the BIOS.
memory.pagefile.off.title: The page file is turned off
memory.pagefile.off.detail: Without a page file, games and programs can crash with "out of memory" errors even when RAM looks free.
memory.pagefile.off.fix: Let Windows manage the page file size (System → Advanced system settings → Performance → Virtual memory).
memory.samechannel.title: The memory modules seem to share one channel
memory.samechannel.detail: All {0} modules are reported in the same memory channel, so the memory may run in single-channel mode with half the bandwidth. This usually happens when the modules sit in neighboring slots.
memory.samechannel.fix: Check the motherboard manual for the recommended slots for {0} modules (usually A2 and B2, the second and fourth slot from the processor) and move the modules there.
memory.top.title: Programs using the most memory: {0}
memory.top.detail: Memory is almost full. These programs use the most of it right now (all their processes added together).
memory.top.fix: Close the programs you don't need, especially browsers with many tabs. If one keeps growing until it is restarted, update or replace it.
memory.pool.leak.title: Drivers are using {0} of memory (non-paged pool)
memory.pool.leak.detail: Drivers normally use a few hundred megabytes. This much usually means a driver keeps taking memory without giving it back (a memory leak); network, VPN, antivirus and RGB lighting drivers are the usual suspects. RAM then fills up over time until the PC slows down or freezes.
memory.pool.leak.fix: Update the network, chipset and graphics drivers and uninstall tools you don't use. A restart frees the memory for a while; if it keeps growing, Microsoft's free PoolMon tool can name the driver.
memory.xmp.off.title: Memory runs below its rated speed ({0} instead of {1} MT/s)
memory.xmp.off.detail: The modules are sold for {1} MT/s but run at {0} MT/s, which usually means XMP/EXPO is off in the BIOS. Faster memory gives more FPS in CPU-limited games.
memory.xmp.off.fix: Turn on XMP (Intel) or EXPO/DOCP (AMD) in the BIOS. If the PC becomes unstable afterwards, turn it off again.
storage.smart.needadmin.title: Disk health (SMART) needs administrator rights
storage.smart.needadmin.detail: Without administrator rights CHC can only show the health status that Windows reports.
storage.smart.needadmin.fix: Restart CHC as administrator to see temperature, life remaining and SMART attributes.
storage.smart.uncorrectable.title: {0}: {1} uncorrectable sectors
storage.smart.uncorrectable.detail: The disk could not read some of its data. This is a strong sign of upcoming failure.
storage.smart.uncorrectable.fix: Back up your data now and plan to replace this disk.
storage.smart.reallocated.title: {0}: {1} reallocated sectors
storage.smart.reallocated.detail: The disk replaced damaged areas with spare ones. A growing number means the disk is wearing out.
storage.smart.reallocated.fix: Back up important data and watch whether this number increases.
storage.smart.pending.title: {0}: {1} sectors waiting to be remapped
storage.smart.pending.detail: These sectors were hard to read and their data may be lost.
storage.smart.pending.fix: Back up your data and run a full disk check (chkdsk /r).
storage.nvme.criticalwarning.title: {0}: the SSD reports a critical warning ({1})
storage.nvme.criticalwarning.detail: The drive itself reports a critical condition (spare space, temperature, reliability or read-only mode).
storage.nvme.criticalwarning.fix: Back up your data immediately and contact the manufacturer.
storage.nvme.mediaerrors.title: {0}: {1} media and data integrity errors
storage.nvme.mediaerrors.detail: The SSD detected errors it could not correct.
storage.nvme.mediaerrors.fix: Back up your data and keep an eye on this drive.
storage.smart.crc.title: {0}: {1} interface (CRC) errors
storage.smart.crc.detail: Transfer errors are usually caused by a bad SATA cable or connection, not by the disk itself.
storage.smart.crc.fix: Replace the SATA cable or try another port.
storage.health.bad.title: {0} is failing
storage.health.bad.detail: SMART data says this disk is in poor health.
storage.health.bad.fix: Back up your data immediately and replace this disk.
storage.health.caution.title: {0} needs attention
storage.health.caution.detail: SMART data shows signs of wear or errors.
storage.health.caution.fix: Back up important data and check the SMART details below.
storage.life.critical.title: {0}: only {1}% life remaining
storage.life.critical.detail: The SSD is close to the end of its rated write endurance.
storage.life.critical.fix: Back up your data and replace the drive soon.
storage.life.low.title: {0}: {1}% life remaining
storage.life.low.detail: The SSD has used most of its rated write endurance.
storage.life.low.fix: Keep backups and consider replacing it in the near future.
storage.temp.critical.title: {0} is very hot ({1} °C)
storage.temp.critical.detail: At this temperature the drive slows down and its lifetime is reduced.
storage.temp.critical.fix: Improve the airflow around the drive or add an M.2 heatsink.
storage.temp.high.title: {0} is running warm ({1} °C)
storage.temp.high.detail: High temperatures make drives throttle and shorten their life.
storage.temp.high.fix: Improve case airflow or add a heatsink.
storage.readerrors.title: {0}: {1} uncorrected read errors
storage.readerrors.detail: Windows recorded read errors that the disk could not correct.
storage.system.hdd.title: Windows is installed on a hard disk ({0})
storage.system.hdd.detail: Mechanical drives are many times slower than SSDs at starting Windows and programs.
storage.system.hdd.fix: Moving Windows to an SSD is the most effective upgrade for an older PC.
storage.disk.ok.life.title: {0} is healthy ({1}% life remaining)
storage.disk.ok.title: {0} is healthy
storage.volume.full.title: Drive {0} is almost full ({1:0.#}% free, {2})
storage.volume.full.detail: Very little free space slows Windows down and can block updates.
storage.volume.full.fix: Delete files you don't need, empty the Recycle Bin or run Disk Cleanup.
storage.volume.low.title: Drive {0} is running out of space ({1:0.#}% free, {2})
storage.volume.low.fix: Free up space with Storage Sense or Disk Cleanup.
storage.events.disk.title: {0} disk errors in the last {1} days
storage.events.disk.detail: Windows logged disk errors such as bad blocks, controller errors or retried transfers.
storage.events.disk.fix: Check the cables and connections, run a disk check and back up important data.
storage.events.ntfs.title: {0} file system errors in the last {1} days
storage.events.ntfs.detail: NTFS reported a damaged file system structure.
storage.resets.title: Disk timeouts in the last {1} days: {0}
storage.resets.detail: The disk controller had to reset a disk. This often feels like a short freeze.
storage.resets.fix: Update the SSD firmware and the chipset/storage drivers, check the SATA cable, and back up important data.
storage.trim.off.title: TRIM is turned off in Windows
storage.trim.off.detail: Without TRIM an SSD doesn't know which data was deleted, so it slows down and wears out faster over time.
storage.trim.off.fix: Run "fsutil behavior set DisableDeleteNotify 0" in an administrator terminal and restart the computer.
storage.hdd.old.title: {0} has been running for {1} hours
storage.hdd.old.detail: That is more than four and a half years of non-stop running. Hard disks wear mechanically and become more likely to fail with age, even when SMART still looks fine.
storage.hdd.old.fix: Keep an up-to-date backup of this disk and plan to replace it, ideally with an SSD.
storage.smart.spinretry.title: {0} had trouble spinning up (retries: {1})
storage.smart.spinretry.detail: The disk did not reach full speed on the first try. This points to a weakening motor or bearing, or to an unstable power supply or cable.
storage.smart.spinretry.fix: Back up this disk now, check its power and data cables, and replace the disk if the number keeps rising.
storage.nvme.overheat.title: {0}: the SSD reports that it is overheating
storage.nvme.overheat.detail: The drive's own temperature warning is on. SSDs slow themselves down when they get too hot, and constant heat shortens their life.
storage.nvme.overheat.fix: Improve the airflow around the drive: fit the motherboard's M.2 heatsink, keep it out of the graphics card's hot exhaust and check the case fans.
gpu.temp.critical.title: {0} is overheating ({1:0} °C)
gpu.temp.critical.detail: The graphics card is close to its thermal limit.
gpu.temp.critical.fix: Clean the graphics card fans and heatsink and improve case airflow.
gpu.temp.high.title: {0} is running hot ({1:0} °C)
gpu.temp.high.fix: Clean the fans and check the case airflow.
gpu.hotspot.high.title: {0}: hot spot temperature is high ({1:0} °C)
gpu.hotspot.high.detail: A big gap between core and hot spot temperature can mean the thermal paste has dried out.
gpu.hotspot.high.fix: Consider having the thermal paste of the graphics card renewed.
gpu.memjunction.high.title: {0}: video memory temperature is high ({1:0} °C)
gpu.memjunction.high.fix: Improve airflow; worn thermal pads may need replacing.
gpu.status.title: {0} reports status "{1}"
gpu.status.detail: Windows reports a problem with this display adapter.
gpu.status.fix: Reinstall or update the graphics driver.
gpu.driver.old.title: {0}: the graphics driver is old ({1})
gpu.driver.old.detail: Newer drivers fix bugs and improve performance and compatibility.
gpu.driver.old.fix: Update the driver from the NVIDIA, AMD or Intel website.
gpu.ok.temp.title: {0} is working normally ({1:0} °C)
gpu.ok.title: {0} is working normally
gpu.resets.title: Graphics driver timeouts in the last {1} days: {0}
gpu.resets.detail: Windows had to reset the graphics driver. Games freeze or the screen goes black for a moment when this happens.
gpu.resets.fix: Clean-install the latest graphics driver, remove any GPU overclock or undervolt, and check the GPU power cables and temperatures.
gpu.livekernel.title: Graphics recoveries by Windows in the last {2} days: {0} ({1})
gpu.livekernel.detail: The graphics driver hung and Windows recovered it without a blue screen.
gpu.livekernel.fix: Update the graphics driver. If it keeps happening, check GPU temperatures and remove any overclock.
gpu.temp.peak.title: {0} reached {1:0} °C while CHC was open
gpu.temp.peak.detail: Graphics cards cool down quickly after a game, so the peak matters more than the current value.
gpu.temp.peak.fix: Clean the fans, improve case airflow or use a more aggressive fan curve.
gpu.hotspot.peak.title: {0}: the hot spot reached {1:0} °C while CHC was open
gpu.hotspot.peak.fix: A high hot spot often means dried-out thermal paste; consider having it renewed.
gpu.nodriver.title: {0} has no graphics driver installed
gpu.nodriver.detail: Windows is using its basic display driver, which has no 3D acceleration: games run very badly or not at all, and the resolution and refresh rate may be limited.
gpu.nodriver.fix: Install the driver from the graphics card maker: NVIDIA (nvidia.com/drivers), AMD (amd.com/support) or Intel (intel.com/support).
gpu.pcie.narrow.title: {0} is connected at PCIe x{1} instead of x{2}
gpu.pcie.narrow.detail: The card supports x{2} but works with fewer lanes, so it has less bandwidth to the processor. Usual reasons: the card sits in a lower slot (often wired as x4), an M.2 drive shares lanes with the slot, or the card isn't fully seated.
gpu.pcie.narrow.fix: Put the card in the top full-length slot, check that it clicks fully into place, and look up in the motherboard manual which M.2 slots share lanes with the graphics slot.
gpu.display.igpu.title: The monitor is connected to the motherboard, not to {0}
gpu.display.igpu.detail: The screen is driven by {1} (the graphics built into the processor) while the graphics card has no monitor connected. Games then run on the much slower built-in graphics.
gpu.display.igpu.fix: Plug the monitor cable into the graphics card's outputs (the lower ports on the back of the PC), not into the motherboard's ports next to the USB connectors.
battery.health.critical.title: The battery is heavily worn ({0:0}% of its original capacity)
battery.health.critical.detail: The battery holds less than half of its original charge.
battery.health.low.title: The battery shows noticeable wear ({0:0}% of its original capacity)
battery.health.low.detail: Battery runtime is much shorter than when it was new.
battery.health.low.fix: Avoid keeping the laptop at 100 % all the time; many manufacturers offer a charge limit option.
battery.health.ok.title: The battery is in good condition ({0:0}% of its original capacity)
battery.health.unknown.title: Battery capacity could not be read
battery.health.unknown.fix: Restart CHC as administrator or run "powercfg /batteryreport".
battery.cycles.high.title: The battery has gone through many charge cycles ({0})
battery.charger.weak.title: The battery is draining while plugged in ({0:0.0} W)
battery.charger.weak.detail: The charger delivers less power than the laptop uses, so the battery makes up the difference and slowly empties even though the laptop is plugged in. Typical causes: a weaker charger than the original, a USB-C charger or cable that can't deliver enough watts, or a worn charger or cable.
battery.charger.weak.fix: Use the original charger, or one with at least the wattage printed on the original. With USB-C, use a charger and cable rated for the laptop's full power (for example 100 W).
battery.wear.fast.title: The battery is wearing out quickly ({0:0.#} points in {1} months)
battery.wear.fast.detail: Batteries normally lose a few percent of their capacity per year. Faster wear comes mostly from heat and from sitting at 100% charge all the time.
battery.wear.fast.fix: If the laptop is mostly plugged in, turn on the charge limit in the manufacturer's app (often 80%). Keep the air vents clear and don't game on a soft surface such as a bed.
board.bios.old.title: The BIOS/UEFI firmware is old ({0})
board.bios.old.detail: Firmware updates often improve stability, compatibility and security.
board.bios.old.fix: Check the support page of your motherboard or laptop manufacturer for updates.
board.secureboot.off.title: Secure Boot is turned off
board.secureboot.off.detail: Secure Boot protects the startup process against malware and is required by the anti-cheat of some games.
board.secureboot.off.fix: You can turn it on in the UEFI settings.
board.tpm.off.title: TPM is not enabled
board.tpm.off.detail: TPM 2.0 is required by Windows 11 and is used by BitLocker and Windows Hello.
board.tpm.off.fix: Enable fTPM (AMD) or PTT (Intel) in the UEFI settings.
board.uptime.long.title: The computer hasn't been restarted for {0} days
board.uptime.long.detail: Long uptimes delay updates and let small problems build up.
board.uptime.long.fix: Restart the computer from time to time.
board.ok.title: No firmware or system issues detected
board.updates.failed.title: An update failed to install {1} times
board.updates.failed.detail: "{0}" failed with error {2} (last {3} days). Until it installs, the fixes it contains are missing.
board.updates.failed.fix: Restart the computer and try again in Settings → Windows Update. If it still fails, run the Windows Update troubleshooter (Settings → System → Troubleshoot) or look up the error code on Microsoft's support site.
board.restart.pending.title: Windows is waiting for a restart to finish installing updates
board.restart.pending.detail: Some updates stay half installed until the computer restarts, and drivers and system files can be in a mixed state until then.
board.restart.pending.fix: Save your work and restart the computer (use Restart, not Shut down).
board.windows.unsupported.title: {0} {1} no longer gets security updates
board.windows.unsupported.detail: Support for this version ended on {2}. Without security updates, newly found security holes stay open, and new games and drivers may stop supporting it.
board.windows.unsupported.fix: Install the latest version of Windows 11 through Settings → Windows Update. If this PC can't run Windows 11, consider upgrading the hardware or moving to a supported operating system.
stability.unavailable.title: The Windows event log could not be read
stability.whea.errors.title: Hardware errors (WHEA) in the last {1} days: {0}
stability.whea.errors.detail: A hardware error could not be corrected. Most errors came from {2}.
stability.whea.errors.fix: Remove overclocks and undervolts, test the memory with Windows Memory Diagnostic and check temperatures.
stability.whea.corrected.title: Corrected hardware errors in the last {1} days: {0}
stability.whea.corrected.detail: Windows corrected these errors automatically, but frequent ones can point to an unstable overclock, PCIe or memory problems. Most came from {2}.
stability.whea.corrected.fix: If the number keeps growing, remove overclocks and check which device the events mention.
stability.bsod.title: Blue screen crashes in the last {1} days: {0}
stability.bsod.detail: Most common error: {2}. It usually points to: {3}.
stability.bsod.fix: Update drivers, remove overclocks and run a memory test. Tools like WhoCrashed help to read the crash dumps.
stability.device.title: Device problem: {0}
stability.device.fix: Open Device Manager and update, reinstall or remove the device.
stability.ok.title: No crashes or hardware errors in the last {0} days
stability.incidents.title: Freezes, crashes and shutdowns
stability.incidents.subtitle: Incidents in the last {1} days: {0}, newest first
stability.incidents.none: No freezes, crashes or sudden shutdowns in the last {0} days.
stability.apps.title: Programs that crashed or froze
stability.apps.subtitle: Last {0} days
stability.power.title: Power and sleep settings
stability.power.subtitle: Power plan: {0}
stability.diagnosis.title: Most problems point to: {0}
stability.diagnosis.detail: {1} of the {2} recent incidents left clues that point here.
stability.forcedoff.title: Freezes that needed the power button in the last {1} days: {0}
stability.forcedoff.detail: Windows stopped responding completely. The table below shows what happened just before each freeze.
stability.forcedoff.fix: Check the likely cause in the table. Typical fixes: update the chipset and graphics drivers and the BIOS, and turn off XMP/EXPO and any undervolt to test.
stability.sleepfail.title: Crashes while going to sleep or waking up in the last {1} days: {0}
stability.sleepfail.detail: A driver failed during a sleep or wake transition.
stability.sleepfail.fix: Update the chipset, graphics and network drivers and the BIOS. If it continues, turn off hybrid sleep and Fast Startup.
stability.silent.title: Shutdowns without warning in the last {1} days: {0}
stability.silent.detail: No crash was recorded. Either the power was cut (power supply, cable, outlet or outage) or Windows froze so completely that it was switched off by force.
stability.silent.fix: If you switched it off because it froze, treat it as a freeze and check the clues below. Otherwise check the power supply and its cables, especially with a powerful graphics card.
stability.livekernel.title: Hardware hangs Windows recovered from in the last {2} days: {0} ({1})
stability.livekernel.detail: A driver or device stopped responding and Windows reset it without a blue screen.
stability.livekernel.fix: Update the chipset driver and the drivers of the device involved.
stability.app.crash.title: {0} crashed {1} times
stability.app.crash.fix: Update or reinstall the program. If it is a game, verify its files in the launcher.
stability.app.crash.gpu.title: {0} crashed {1} times inside the {2}
stability.app.crash.gpu.detail: The crashes happened in graphics driver code, which points to the driver, an unstable GPU overclock or the graphics card itself.
stability.app.crash.gpu.fix: Clean-install the latest driver (for example with DDU), remove any GPU overclock and check the graphics card's power cables.
stability.app.hang.title: {0} stopped responding {1} times
stability.thermal.title: Overheating shutdowns in the last {1} days: {0}
stability.thermal.detail: Windows shut the computer down (or hibernated it) because a temperature sensor reached its critical limit. This protects the hardware, but it means the cooling can't keep up.
stability.thermal.fix: Clean the dust out of the fans and heatsinks, check that every fan spins and make sure the case gets enough air. On a laptop, keep the vents free and use it on a hard surface. If the processor cooler was taken off recently, renew the thermal paste.
stability.network.title: Network adapter resets in the last {3} days: {1}
stability.network.detail: "{0}" stopped responding and Windows had to reset it (separate episodes: {2}). Every reset drops the connection for a moment, which shows up as lag spikes or disconnects in online games.
stability.network.fix: Install the latest network driver from the chip maker (Realtek, Intel, Killer) or from your motherboard's support page, turn off "Energy-Efficient Ethernet" / "Green Ethernet" in the adapter's advanced settings, and try another cable or port. If it continues, set PCI Express power saving to Off.

incident.forcedoff: Froze and was turned off with the power button
incident.sleep: Crashed while going to sleep or waking up
incident.silent: Shut off without warning (power cut or total freeze)
cause.hardware: Unstable hardware (processor, memory or a PCIe device)
cause.storage: A disk or the disk controller
cause.silent: Power supply, power cut or a total freeze
cause.unknown: No clear cause in the logs
cause.gpu.fix: Clean-install the latest graphics driver (for example with DDU), remove any GPU overclock or undervolt, and check the graphics card's power cables and temperatures.
cause.memory.fix: Turn off XMP/EXPO in the BIOS to test, run Windows Memory Diagnostic, and if errors remain test the modules one by one.
cause.cpu.fix: Remove any CPU overclock or undervolt (including Curve Optimizer), update the BIOS and check the CPU cooler.
cause.hardware.fix: Set the BIOS to default settings (no overclock, no XMP/EXPO) to test, update the BIOS and chipset driver, and check temperatures.
cause.storage.fix: Back up your data, update the SSD firmware and storage drivers, check the cable, and look at the disk's SMART details on the Storage page.
cause.driver.fix: Update the chipset, graphics, network and audio drivers. If the problem started after a driver update, roll that driver back.
cause.sleep.fix: Update the BIOS, chipset and graphics drivers. If it continues, turn off hybrid sleep and Fast Startup, and set PCI Express power saving to Off.
cause.lowmemory.fix: Find the program that keeps using more memory (Task Manager → Memory), close it or update it, and let Windows manage the page file.
cause.system.fix: Run "sfc /scannow" and "DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth" in an administrator terminal.
cause.silent.fix: If you turned it off because it froze: set the BIOS to defaults (no XMP/EXPO, no undervolt), update the BIOS and chipset driver, and check the power-saving tips. If it simply lost power: check the power supply, its cables and the outlet; high-end graphics cards need a strong, good-quality PSU.
cause.unknown.fix: Note what you were doing when it happened; after a few more incidents CHC can usually narrow it down.
cause.heat.fix: Clean the fans and heatsinks, check that all fans spin and the case gets enough air, and renew the processor's thermal paste if it is old. Watch the temperatures on the Sensors page while gaming.
clue.appcrash.gpu: {0} crashed in the graphics driver at {1}

power.aspm.title: PCI Express power saving is on
power.aspm.detail: Link State Power Management can cause graphics driver resets and freezes on some PCs.
power.aspm.fix: Set "PCI Express → Link State Power Management" to Off in the advanced power plan settings.
power.faststartup.title: Fast Startup is on
power.faststartup.detail: Fast Startup keeps drivers half asleep between shutdowns and can cause freezes on some systems.
power.faststartup.fix: Turn it off in Control Panel → Power Options → "Choose what the power buttons do".
power.hybridsleep.title: Hybrid sleep is on
power.hybridsleep.detail: Hybrid sleep combines sleep and hibernation and fails on some desktop PCs.
power.hybridsleep.fix: Turn off "Allow hybrid sleep" in the advanced power plan settings.
power.modernstandby.title: This PC uses Modern Standby
power.modernstandby.detail: With Modern Standby the PC keeps working in the background while asleep, which some drivers handle badly.
power.modernstandby.fix: Update the BIOS and drivers. If wake problems continue, ask the manufacturer about classic (S3) sleep.
power.usbsuspend.title: USB selective suspend is on
power.usbsuspend.detail: Some USB devices fail to wake up again, which can freeze the PC during sleep.
power.usbsuspend.fix: Turn off "USB selective suspend" in the advanced power plan settings.
perf.page.subtitle: Measure FPS while you play and find out what holds your games back.
perf.howto: Press Start, switch to your game and play for at least two minutes, then come back and press Stop.
perf.status.waiting: Waiting for a game… switch to your game now
perf.needadmin: Measuring FPS needs administrator rights. Without them CHC only records loads and temperatures.
perf.summary.none: No game measured yet. The checks below apply to every game.
perf.session.subtitle: Measured {0} · {1}
perf.table.background: Other programs using the CPU while you played
perf.settings.title: Before you play
perf.settings.subtitle: Windows and display settings that affect every game
perf.stuttercause.disk: heavy disk activity (the game loading data)
perf.stuttercause.unknown: nothing obvious (often shader compilation or the game itself)
perf.refresh.low.title: Your monitor runs at {0} Hz but supports {1} Hz
perf.refresh.low.detail: You only see as many frames per second as the refresh rate allows, so games look less smooth than they could.
perf.refresh.low.fix: Settings → System → Display → Advanced display → choose {1} Hz. Also make sure the cable (DisplayPort/HDMI) supports it.
perf.powersaver.title: The power plan "{0}" slows the PC down
perf.powersaver.detail: Power saver limits the processor's speed.
perf.powersaver.fix: Switch to "Balanced" or "High performance" in Settings → System → Power.
perf.gamemode.off.title: Game Mode is off
perf.gamemode.off.detail: Game Mode gives the game priority and pauses background updates while you play.
perf.gamemode.off.fix: Turn it on in Settings → Gaming → Game Mode.
perf.nofps.title: FPS could not be measured
perf.nofps.detail: Measuring frames needs administrator rights and a DirectX game. Loads and temperatures were still recorded.
perf.nofps.fix: Run CHC as administrator and measure again.
perf.tooshort.title: The session was too short to analyse
perf.tooshort.fix: Play for at least one or two minutes before pressing Stop.
perf.cpubound.title: The processor limited the FPS {0:0}% of the time
perf.cpubound.detail: The graphics card was waiting for the processor (average CPU load {1:0}%).
perf.cpubound.fix: Lower CPU-heavy settings (view distance, crowds, physics), close background programs, and make sure memory runs in dual channel with XMP/EXPO.
perf.cpubound.single.title: One processor core limited the FPS {0:0}% of the time
perf.cpubound.single.detail: The game leans on a single thread: one core was at its limit while the processor as a whole was only {1:0}% busy. This is typical for many games.
perf.cpubound.single.fix: Lower CPU-heavy settings, close background programs and keep the processor cool. Faster memory or a CPU with stronger single-core speed helps most.
perf.singlechannel.title: Single-channel memory costs FPS here
perf.singlechannel.detail: With one memory module the processor gets half the memory bandwidth, which matters most when a game is CPU limited.
perf.singlechannel.fix: Add a second identical module for dual-channel mode.
perf.gpubound.title: The graphics card was fully used {0:0}% of the time
perf.gpubound.detail: This is normal: the graphics card is the limit.
perf.gpubound.fix: For more FPS, lower graphics settings or resolution, or turn on DLSS, FSR or XeSS.
perf.capped.title: FPS was capped at about {0} for {1:0}% of the session
perf.capped.detail: VSync or a frame limiter kept the frame rate steady. This is not a problem.
perf.capped.fix: If you want more FPS, raise or remove the limit in the game or driver settings.
perf.cpu.thermal.title: The processor overheated ({0:0} °C) and slowed down by {1:0}%
perf.cpu.thermal.detail: At its temperature limit the processor lowers its clock speed to protect itself.
perf.cpu.thermal.fix: Improve cooling: clean the cooler, check its mounting and thermal paste, and improve case airflow.
perf.cpu.hot.title: The processor ran at its temperature limit ({0:0} °C)
perf.cpu.hot.detail: Some processors are designed to run this hot, but better cooling usually gives a little more speed.
perf.gpu.thermal.title: The graphics card got hot ({0:0} °C) and slowed down by {1:0}%
perf.gpu.thermal.detail: The card lowered its clock speed because of the temperature.
perf.gpu.thermal.fix: Clean the fans, improve case airflow or use a more aggressive fan curve.
perf.gpu.hot.title: The graphics card ran hot ({0:0} °C)
perf.gpu.hot.fix: Keep an eye on airflow and dust in the fans.
perf.gpu.powerlimit.title: The graphics card was at its power limit {0:0}% of the time
perf.gpu.powerlimit.detail: Under full load many cards run at their power limit. This is normal, not a fault.
perf.vram.full.title: Video memory was full ({0:0.0} of {1:0.0} GB)
perf.vram.full.detail: When VRAM runs out the game has to move data over the slower PCIe bus, which causes stutters.
perf.ram.full.title: RAM was almost full while you played ({0:0}%)
perf.ram.full.detail: When memory is this full, Windows starts moving data to the disk, which causes stutters.
perf.ram.full.fix: Close browsers and other programs while gaming, or add RAM.
perf.stutter.title: Stutters: {0} ({1:0.#} per minute)
perf.stutter.detail: A stutter is a frame that takes much longer than the ones around it. Most stutters came together with {2}.
perf.stutter.fix: Check the related findings above, keep the game on an SSD and update the graphics driver.
perf.background.title: {0} used {1:0.#}% CPU while you played
perf.background.detail: Background programs take processor time away from the game.
perf.background.fix: Close it while gaming, or check why it is so busy.
perf.game.hdd.title: {0} is installed on a hard disk ({1})
perf.game.hdd.detail: Loading from a hard disk means long loading times and stutters whenever the game streams data.
perf.game.hdd.fix: Move the game to an SSD.
perf.good.title: No performance problems found ({0:0} FPS on average)
perf.ram.peak.title: RAM briefly filled up while you played ({0:0}%)
perf.ram.peak.detail: At the peak, {0:0}% of the {1} of RAM was in use. When memory runs out, Windows moves data to the disk, which shows up as sudden hitches.
perf.ram.peak.fix: Close browsers and other programs before playing. If it happens in every game, more RAM (or a second module for dual channel) helps.
perf.lows.title: Uneven frame times (1% low {0:0} FPS, average {1:0} FPS)
perf.lows.detail: The slowest frames are much slower than the average, so the game can feel less smooth than the FPS counter suggests.
perf.lows.fix: Limit the frame rate a little below what your PC reaches (with the in-game limiter or the graphics driver), close background programs and update the graphics driver.
perf.cpu.maxstate.title: The power plan limits the processor to {0}%
perf.cpu.maxstate.detail: "Maximum processor state" is set below 100%, which usually turns off the processor's boost clock and costs a lot of performance.
perf.cpu.maxstate.fix: Set "Processor power management → Maximum processor state" to 100% in the advanced power plan settings, or choose the Balanced or High performance plan.
perf.cpu.boostoff.title: Processor boost is turned off in the power plan
perf.cpu.boostoff.detail: "Processor performance boost mode" is set to Disabled, so the processor never goes above its base clock. That costs a lot of FPS.
perf.cpu.boostoff.fix: Choose the Balanced or High performance plan, or run "powercfg /setacvalueindex SCHEME_CURRENT SUB_PROCESSOR PERFBOOSTMODE 2" and then "powercfg /setactive SCHEME_CURRENT" in an administrator terminal.
perf.rebar.off.title: Resizable BAR is off for {0}
perf.rebar.off.detail: The card supports Resizable BAR, which lets the processor reach all of the video memory at once. Some games run noticeably faster with it, and Intel Arc cards depend on it.
perf.rebar.off.fix: In the BIOS, turn on "Above 4G Decoding" and "Re-Size BAR Support" (this needs UEFI boot with CSM off), and keep the BIOS and graphics driver up to date.
perf.hags.framegen.title: Hardware-accelerated GPU scheduling is off
perf.hags.framegen.detail: DLSS Frame Generation on {0} needs it, so games won't offer frame generation until it is turned on.
perf.hags.framegen.fix: Turn it on in Settings → System → Display → Graphics → Change default graphics settings, then restart the computer.
perf.gamedvr.title: Background recording (Xbox Game Bar) is on
perf.gamedvr.detail: Windows keeps recording the last minutes of gameplay all the time, which costs a few FPS and keeps writing to the disk.
perf.gamedvr.fix: Turn off Settings → Gaming → Captures → "Record what happened". You can still record clips by hand.
perf.hvci.title: Memory Integrity (core isolation) is on
perf.hvci.detail: It protects Windows against attacks through drivers, but it can cost some performance in games, usually a few percent.
perf.hvci.fix: If you prefer maximum performance over this extra protection, turn it off in Windows Security → Device security → Core isolation details, then restart. Leaving it on is the safer choice.
perf.online.title: {0} is an online game: ping {1:0} ms, jitter {2:0.#} ms, packet loss {3:0.#}%
perf.online.detail: CHC saw the game exchanging data with servers on the internet and measured the connection while you played (ping to {4}). Stutters are frames the PC drew late; lag is a delay on the connection. Both are explained separately.
perf.server.silent.title: The game server doesn't answer pings
perf.server.silent.detail: The game plays on {0}, but that server ignores pings, so the ping shown is to 1.1.1.1. The game's own network display may show slightly different numbers.
perf.server.high.title: The ping to the game server is high ({0:0} ms)
perf.server.high.detail: The internet itself answered in {1:0} ms, so most of the delay is the distance to the game server.
perf.server.high.fix: Choose a server or region closer to you in the game's settings, and turn off any VPN while playing.
perf.server.loss.title: Packets were lost on the way to the game server ({0:0.#}%)
perf.server.loss.detail: The connection to the rest of the internet had no loss, so the problem lies on the route to this server or at the server itself, not in your home.
perf.server.loss.fix: Try another server or region. If it happens with every server of this game, report it to your internet provider together with the results.
perf.network.title: Connection during the game
perf.status.measuring.online: Measuring {0} · {1} · online game, the ping is measured too
perf.battery.title: The game ran on battery ({0:0}% of the session)
perf.battery.detail: On battery, laptops cut the power of the processor and graphics card to make the battery last, so games run noticeably slower than when plugged in.
perf.battery.fix: Plug in the charger while gaming, then measure again to see the laptop's real performance.
perf.charger.weak.title: The charger couldn't keep up: the battery drained while plugged in ({0:0.0} W from the battery)
perf.charger.weak.detail: During the game the laptop used more power than the charger supplies, so the battery made up the difference (the charge fell by {1:0.#} points). When the battery runs low, the laptop slows the game down to save power.
perf.charger.weak.fix: Use the original charger, or one with at least the wattage printed on it. Many gaming laptops need their full-power barrel charger; USB-C chargers often deliver only 65–100 W.
perf.power.title: The PC drew about {0:0} W at its peak while gaming
perf.power.detail: Measured: the processor and the graphics card. The motherboard, memory, disks and fans can't report their power, so about {1:0} W is added for them. The graphics card's very short spikes can go well above these figures.
perf.power.fix: A good-quality power supply (80 PLUS Gold or better, from a known brand) of at least {2} W suits this PC. This includes headroom for heavier games, short power spikes and ageing.
perf.power.laptop.title: The laptop drew about {0:0} W on average while gaming
perf.power.laptop.detail: This is the measured power of the processor and graphics card plus an estimate for the screen and the rest of the laptop. The charger must supply at least this much, otherwise the battery makes up the difference.
perf.psu.shutdowns.title: Sudden power-offs and a power-hungry PC: check the power supply
perf.psu.shutdowns.detail: The PC switched off without a crash record, as if the power was cut (sudden shutdowns: {0}), and in this game it draws up to about {1:0} W. A power supply that is too weak, old or of poor quality switches off when the graphics card demands a burst of power.
perf.psu.shutdowns.fix: Check that the power supply has at least {2} W and is of good quality, that the graphics card's power cables are pushed in fully, and that each power socket on the card has its own cable from the power supply (no splitter or daisy chain).
perf.spec.fullruntime: A full charge lasts in this game
perf.gameset.title: Game settings
perf.gameset.source: Read from the game's own settings ({0}, {1})
perf.gameset.nosource: The game's settings file was not found; only its window and the monitor were measured.
perf.game.cpuheavy.generic: view distance, crowd density and physics
perf.game.lowhz.title: {0} ran with the monitor at {1} Hz instead of {2} Hz
perf.game.lowhz.detail: The game's own fullscreen mode picked a lower refresh rate, so you see fewer frames than the monitor can show and motion looks less smooth.
perf.game.lowhz.fix: In the game's display settings set the refresh rate to {2} Hz, or switch to borderless (windowed fullscreen), which uses the desktop's refresh rate.
perf.game.resolution.title: {0} renders at {1} on a {2} monitor
perf.game.resolution.detail: A lower resolution than the monitor's is stretched to fill the screen and looks blurry. It does give more FPS when the graphics card is the limit.
perf.game.resolution.fix: Use {2}. If you need the FPS, turn on DLSS, FSR or XeSS (or lower the render scale) instead: the image stays sharper and the interface stays crisp.
perf.game.windowed.title: {0} ran in a window
perf.game.windowed.detail: In a window with a title bar the desktop composes the game's frames, which can add input delay, and some games then don't use G-Sync or FreeSync.
perf.game.windowed.fix: Choose Fullscreen or Borderless (windowed fullscreen) in the game's display settings.
perf.game.vsync.title: VSync is on in {0}
perf.game.vsync.detail: VSync holds the frame rate at the monitor's {1} Hz and adds input delay; when the FPS drops below that, the game can stutter.
perf.game.vsync.fix: With a G-Sync or FreeSync monitor, turn VSync off in the game and limit FPS to {2} instead. Without one, keep VSync only if screen tearing bothers you more than input delay.
perf.game.fpslimit.title: {0} limits FPS to {1} on a {2} Hz monitor
perf.game.fpslimit.detail: The graphics card still had room, so the limit, not the hardware, held the frame rate down.
perf.game.fpslimit.fix: Raise the game's frame limit to {2} (or {3} with G-Sync/FreeSync) for smoother motion.
perf.game.renderscale.low.title: {0} renders at {1:0}% of the screen resolution
perf.game.renderscale.low.detail: A render scale below 100% makes the picture blurry.
perf.game.renderscale.low.fix: Set it to 100% and use DLSS, FSR or XeSS if you need the FPS: they look sharper at the same speed.
perf.game.renderscale.high.title: {0} renders at {1:0}% of the screen resolution
perf.game.renderscale.high.detail: Above 100% the game renders more pixels than the screen has. It looks smoother but costs a lot of FPS, and the graphics card is the limit here.
perf.game.renderscale.high.fix: Set the render scale to 100% for a large FPS gain.
perf.game.gpuheavy.title: For more than {0:0} FPS, lower these settings first: {1}
perf.game.gpuheavy.detail: The graphics card was the limit. These settings are at High or above and cost the most FPS for the least visible difference.
perf.game.gpuheavy.fix: Lower each of them one step and measure again. Shadows, global illumination, effects and post-processing usually give the most FPS back.
perf.game.upscaler.title: Upscaling is off in {0}
perf.game.upscaler.detail: Upscaling renders at a lower resolution and rebuilds a sharp image; in Quality mode it often gives a lot more FPS with little visible difference.
perf.game.upscaler.fix: In the game's graphics settings turn on {1} in Quality mode.
perf.game.reflex.title: NVIDIA Reflex is off in {0}
perf.game.reflex.detail: When the graphics card is the limit, Reflex noticeably cuts input delay at almost no FPS cost.
perf.game.reflex.fix: Set NVIDIA Reflex Low Latency to On (or On + Boost) in the game's settings.
perf.game.cpuheadroom.title: The graphics card had spare power ({0:0}% average load)
perf.game.cpuheadroom.detail: The processor was the limit, so settings that only load the graphics card cost little or no FPS here.
perf.game.cpuheadroom.fix: You can raise textures, anti-aliasing or resolution for a better picture at about the same FPS. For more FPS, lower what loads the processor: {1}.
perf.game.textures.title: {0}: texture quality {1} doesn't fit in the graphics card's memory
perf.game.textures.detail: When video memory is full, textures are moved back and forth over PCI Express, which causes stutters.
perf.game.textures.fix: Lower texture quality one step; it frees the most video memory for the smallest visible difference.
net.page.subtitle: Measure ping, jitter and packet loss and find out where lag comes from.
net.howto: Press Start and leave it running for at least a minute; to catch lag while gaming, start it and then play. CHC pings your router and the public servers 1.1.1.1 and 8.8.8.8 a few times a second.
net.needadmin: Without administrator rights CHC measures the connection but can't tell which programs are using the internet.
net.summary.none: No test has run yet. The connection settings below are checked anyway.
net.session.title: Network test
net.table.programs: Programs using the internet during the test
net.offline.title: No internet connection was found
net.offline.detail: No network adapter has a route to the internet (no router address).
net.offline.fix: Check the cable or Wi-Fi connection and restart the router. If other devices work, run the network troubleshooter in Settings → Network & internet.
net.vpn.title: Internet traffic goes through a VPN
net.vpn.detail: "{0}" routes the connection through a VPN server, which adds distance and usually raises the ping in games.
net.vpn.fix: Disconnect the VPN while gaming, or exclude the game in the VPN's split-tunneling settings.
net.wifi.title: The computer is connected over Wi-Fi
net.wifi.detail: Wi-Fi shares the air with neighbors and other devices, so its ping jumps around much more than a cable's.
net.wifi.fix: For gaming, use a network cable if you can. Otherwise keep the PC close to the router and use the 5 GHz band.
net.wifi.signal.title: The Wi-Fi signal is weak ({0}%)
net.wifi.signal.detail: With a weak signal the connection slows down and has to resend data, which causes lag spikes and packet loss.
net.wifi.signal.fix: Move the PC or the router so fewer walls are in between, point the antennas upward, or use a cable, a mesh system or a powerline adapter.
net.wifi.band24.title: Wi-Fi uses the crowded 2.4 GHz band
net.wifi.band24.detail: 2.4 GHz reaches far but is shared with neighbors' networks, Bluetooth and microwaves, so ping becomes uneven.
net.wifi.band24.fix: Connect to your router's 5 GHz network (often the name ending in "5G") if the signal is good enough where the PC stands.
net.wifi.powersave.title: Wi-Fi power saving is on
net.wifi.powersave.detail: In power saving mode the Wi-Fi adapter naps between packets, which adds delay and makes ping uneven.
net.wifi.powersave.fix: Set "Wireless Adapter Settings → Power Saving Mode" to Maximum Performance in the advanced power plan settings.
net.link.slow.title: The network cable connection runs at {0} instead of {1}
net.link.slow.detail: The adapter supports {1} but agreed on only {0} with the router. Usually the cable is damaged or old (Cat 5), a plug is loose, or the router or switch port only does 100 Mbps. Ping is barely affected, but downloads are capped.
net.link.slow.fix: Try a different Cat 5e or Cat 6 cable and another port on the router, and check that "Speed & Duplex" is set to Auto Negotiation in the adapter's advanced settings.
net.link.halfduplex.title: The network connection runs in half duplex
net.link.halfduplex.detail: In half duplex the adapter can't send and receive at the same time, which causes collisions, packet loss and lag on a modern network.
net.link.halfduplex.fix: Set "Speed & Duplex" back to Auto Negotiation in the adapter's advanced settings and replace the cable if it continues.
net.powersaving.title: Energy-saving options of the network adapter are on
net.powersaving.detail: Energy-Efficient Ethernet, Green Ethernet and similar options on "{0}" put the link to sleep between packets. On some adapters and routers this causes dropouts, resets and a slower link.
net.powersaving.fix: In Device Manager → Network adapters → the adapter → Advanced, turn off Energy-Efficient Ethernet, Green Ethernet and Power Saving Mode.
net.dns.timeouts.title: DNS timeouts in the last {1} days: {0}
net.dns.timeouts.detail: Windows often waited in vain for the DNS server, so websites and game servers were slow to connect.
net.dns.timeouts.fix: Restart the router. If it keeps happening, set a public DNS server such as 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8 in the adapter's IPv4 settings.
net.tooshort.title: The test was too short
net.tooshort.detail: At least 15 seconds are needed for reliable results.
net.tooshort.fix: Run the test again for a minute or longer.
net.nointernet.title: The internet servers didn't answer
net.nointernet.detail: Neither 1.1.1.1 nor 8.8.8.8 answered a single ping. Either the internet is down or a firewall blocks pings.
net.nointernet.fix: Check that websites open. If they do, a firewall or the router blocks pings and the test can't measure the connection.
net.gateway.silent.title: The router doesn't answer pings
net.gateway.silent.detail: Some routers ignore pings, so CHC can't measure the part between the PC and the router separately. The internet measurements are still valid.
net.loss.local.title: Packets are lost between the PC and the router ({0:0.#}%)
net.loss.local.detail: Even the router, the closest device, didn't answer every ping. The problem is inside your home: Wi-Fi, a cable, the network adapter or the router itself.
net.loss.local.fix: Use a cable instead of Wi-Fi (or move closer to the router), try another cable and port, restart the router, and update the network driver.
net.loss.internet.title: Packets are lost on the internet connection ({0:0.#}%)
net.loss.internet.detail: The router answered every ping, but both public servers lost some. The loss happens beyond your router, on the internet provider's line.
net.loss.internet.fix: Restart the modem/router. If it continues, run the test a few times at different hours and show the results to your internet provider.
net.jitter.local.title: The connection to the router is unstable (jitter {0:0.#} ms)
net.jitter.local.detail: Even the router answers unevenly (95% of answers under {1:0} ms), so the lag starts inside your home.
net.jitter.local.fix: Check the network cable and port, update the network driver, and restart the router.
net.jitter.local.wifi.title: The Wi-Fi connection to the router is unstable (jitter {0:0.#} ms)
net.jitter.local.wifi.detail: Even the router answers unevenly over Wi-Fi (95% of answers under {1:0} ms). Interference, distance or a busy channel are the usual reasons.
net.jitter.local.wifi.fix: Use a network cable for gaming, or move closer to the router, switch to 5 GHz and let the router pick a less crowded channel.
net.jitter.internet.title: The ping fluctuates on the internet connection (jitter {0:0.#} ms)
net.jitter.internet.detail: The router answers evenly, but the ping to the internet goes up and down. The fluctuation comes from the internet provider's line or route.
net.jitter.internet.fix: Check whether other devices at home are streaming or downloading during the test. If not, restart the modem and report it to your provider if it continues.
net.spikes.title: Lag spikes: {0} ({1:0.#} per minute)
net.spikes.detail: A lag spike is a ping far above the usual one; in games it feels like rubber-banding or a short freeze. Most likely cause: {2}.
net.spikes.fix: Check the related findings above. Pause downloads and streams on all devices while gaming.
net.spikecause.local: a problem between the PC and the router (Wi-Fi or cable)
net.spikecause.busy: heavy traffic on the connection (a download or upload)
net.spikecause.isp: the internet provider (nothing at home coincided with the spikes)
net.bufferbloat.title: Ping rises when the connection is busy ({0:0} → {1:0} ms)
net.bufferbloat.detail: While something downloaded or uploaded, the ping went from about {0:0} ms to {1:0} ms. The router queues the game's data behind the download ("bufferbloat").
net.bufferbloat.fix: Pause downloads, updates and cloud sync while gaming (Steam, Windows Update, OneDrive...). If the router supports SQM, Smart Queue or QoS, turn it on.
net.latency.high.title: The ping to the internet is high ({0:0} ms)
net.latency.high.detail: {1} usually answers within 5-30 ms. Higher values point to a long route, a mobile or satellite connection, or a VPN.
net.latency.high.fix: If you use a VPN, turn it off. Otherwise ask your provider about the latency; with mobile internet, a better spot for the modem can help.
net.dns.failed.title: DNS lookups failed: {0} of {1}
net.dns.failed.detail: The DNS server didn't answer some lookups, so websites and game servers sometimes fail to connect at first.
net.dns.failed.fix: Set a public DNS server such as 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8 in the adapter's IPv4 settings and restart the router.
net.dns.slow.title: DNS lookups are slow ({0:0} ms)
net.dns.slow.detail: Every new connection starts with a DNS lookup; slow answers make websites and launchers feel sluggish (it doesn't affect ping inside a game).
net.dns.slow.fix: Try a public DNS server such as 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8 in the adapter's IPv4 settings.
net.programs.title: Programs using the internet during the test: {0}
net.programs.detail: These programs sent or received the most data while the test ran. Background downloads and uploads are a common cause of lag.
net.programs.fix: Close or pause the ones you don't need while gaming, and limit download speeds in launchers such as Steam.
net.good.title: The connection is stable (ping {0:0} ms, jitter {1:0.#} ms, loss {2:0.#}%)
net.good.detail: No packet loss, lag spikes or fluctuation worth mentioning were measured during the test.

history.empty.detail: CHC records while it runs, with the window open or in the notification area. Set it to start with Windows in Settings to fill the gaps.

stability.afterchange.title: The problems started after a change: {0}
stability.afterchange.detail: {1} freezes or crashes came in the ten days after it ({2}), none in the two weeks before. A change that lines up like this is the first thing to undo.
stability.afterchange.fix.driver: Roll the driver back (Device Manager → the device → Properties → Driver → Roll Back Driver) or install the previous version; for a graphics card, a clean install with DDU.
stability.afterchange.fix.update: Uninstall the update (Settings → Windows Update → Update history → Uninstall updates), then pause updates until a fixed one comes out.
stability.afterchange.fix.bios: Load the BIOS defaults (Optimized Defaults), turn XMP/EXPO back on and test. If the problems stay, look for a newer BIOS from the board maker or go back to the previous one.
stability.afterchange.fix.memory: Turn XMP/EXPO off or choose a lower memory speed in the BIOS, then test the memory (for example with MemTest86).
stability.afterchange.fix.other: Undo the change if you can and see whether the problems stop.

perf.refresh.low.steps:
Right-click the desktop and choose Display settings.
Scroll down and open Advanced display.
Under "Choose a refresh rate" pick {1} Hz.
If {1} Hz isn't offered, use a DisplayPort cable (or an HDMI 2.0/2.1 cable) and plug it into the graphics card.
perf.refresh.low.why: The monitor can only show as many frames per second as its refresh rate. At {0} Hz every frame above {0} FPS is wasted, and motion looks less smooth than the monitor allows. Windows sometimes falls back to a low rate after a driver update or with an older cable.
perf.gamemode.off.steps:
Open Settings (Windows + I).
Go to Gaming → Game Mode.
Turn Game Mode on.
perf.gamemode.off.why: With Game Mode Windows gives the game's threads priority, holds back Windows Update installs and driver installs, and stops restart notifications while you play. The gain is small on a fast PC but helps against sudden stutters from background work.
perf.hags.framegen.steps:
Open Settings → System → Display → Graphics.
Click "Change default graphics settings" (on newer Windows: Advanced graphics settings).
Turn on "Hardware-accelerated GPU scheduling".
Restart the computer.
In the game, turn on DLSS Frame Generation.
perf.hags.framegen.why: Frame Generation inserts generated frames between the real ones, and that only works when the graphics card schedules its own work. Without this setting games simply hide the option, so a card that could double its frame rate never gets the chance.
perf.hvci.steps:
Open Windows Security (search for it in Start).
Go to Device security → Core isolation details.
Turn Memory integrity off.
Restart the computer.
perf.hvci.why: Memory Integrity runs part of Windows in a separate, protected area so that a malicious driver can't take over the system. Checking every driver this way costs some processor time, which shows as a few percent fewer FPS in some games. It is a trade-off: turning it off makes the PC a little faster and a little less protected, and some anti-cheat systems require it on.
perf.gamedvr.steps:
Open Settings → Gaming → Captures.
Turn off "Record what happened".
To keep recording clips by hand, press Windows + Alt + R when you want to.
perf.gamedvr.why: To be able to save "the last 30 seconds", Windows records every game all the time and throws most of it away. That keeps the graphics card's video encoder and the disk busy, costs a few FPS and can cause small stutters on slower PCs.
perf.powersaver.steps:
Open Settings → System → Power & battery (on a desktop: Power).
Under Power mode choose "Balanced" or "Best performance".
On older Windows: Control Panel → Power Options → choose Balanced or High performance.
perf.powersaver.why: Power saver keeps the processor at low clock speeds and makes it slow to speed up, which saves electricity but costs a lot of performance in games and heavy programs. Balanced already lets the processor boost when needed and save power when idle, so it is the right choice for almost every PC.
perf.cpu.boostoff.steps:
Press Windows + R, type control powercfg.cpl and press Enter.
Click "Change plan settings" next to the active plan, then "Change advanced power settings".
Open Processor power management → Processor performance boost mode.
Set it to Enabled (or Aggressive) and click OK.
Or choose the Balanced plan, which has boost on.
perf.cpu.boostoff.why: Boost (Turbo Boost on Intel, Precision Boost on AMD) lets the processor run well above its base clock whenever it is cool enough, often 30 to 60 percent faster. With boost disabled it never leaves the base clock, so games and programs run much slower. Some "battery saver" tools and tweak guides turn it off without saying so.
perf.cpu.maxstate.steps:
Press Windows + R, type control powercfg.cpl and press Enter.
Click "Change plan settings" next to the active plan, then "Change advanced power settings".
Open Processor power management → Maximum processor state.
Set both values (On battery and Plugged in) to 100% and click OK.
perf.cpu.maxstate.why: "Maximum processor state" below 100% doesn't just shave off a few percent: on most processors any value under 100% switches the boost clock off entirely. It is a common leftover from tools that try to keep laptops cool or quiet.
power.aspm.steps:
Press Windows + R, type control powercfg.cpl and press Enter.
Click "Change plan settings" next to the active plan, then "Change advanced power settings".
Open PCI Express → Link State Power Management.
Set it to Off and click OK.
power.aspm.why: This setting puts the link to the graphics card, NVMe drives and other PCIe devices into a low-power state when they are briefly idle. Waking the link back up takes a moment, and some cards and drivers handle that badly, which shows as driver resets, black screens or freezes. On a desktop the power saved is tiny.
power.faststartup.steps:
Press Windows + R, type control powercfg.cpl and press Enter.
Click "Choose what the power buttons do" on the left.
Click "Change settings that are currently unavailable".
Untick "Turn on fast startup (recommended)" and click Save changes.
power.faststartup.why: With Fast Startup, "Shut down" doesn't really shut Windows down: the kernel and drivers are saved to disk and restored at the next start. Drivers that misbehave are never fully reset, and problems survive shutdowns (only Restart clears them). Turning it off costs a few seconds at start-up on an SSD.
power.hybridsleep.steps:
Press Windows + R, type control powercfg.cpl and press Enter.
Click "Change plan settings" next to the active plan, then "Change advanced power settings".
Open Sleep → Allow hybrid sleep.
Set it to Off and click OK.
power.hybridsleep.why: Hybrid sleep writes the whole memory to disk every time the PC goes to sleep, so that nothing is lost on a power cut. It makes falling asleep slower and depends on every driver handling both sleep and hibernation, which is where some desktop PCs fail and then can't wake up.
power.usbsuspend.steps:
Press Windows + R, type control powercfg.cpl and press Enter.
Click "Change plan settings" next to the active plan, then "Change advanced power settings".
Open USB settings → USB selective suspend setting.
Set it to Disabled and click OK.
power.usbsuspend.why: Selective suspend switches idle USB devices off to save power. Some mice, headsets, controllers and hubs don't come back properly, which shows as devices that stop responding until replugged, or as a PC that freezes while sleeping. On a desktop it saves almost nothing.
memory.pagefile.off.steps:
Press Windows + R, type sysdm.cpl and press Enter.
Open the Advanced tab and click Settings under Performance.
Open the Advanced tab and click Change under Virtual memory.
Tick "Automatically manage paging file size for all drives" and click OK.
Restart the computer.
memory.pagefile.off.why: Windows promises memory to programs up to RAM plus page file, even when most of it is never used. Without a page file that limit is just the RAM, so games and browsers can fail with "out of memory" while Task Manager still shows free memory. An SSD page file costs nothing until it is needed.
storage.trim.off.steps:
Right-click Start and open Terminal (Admin).
Type fsutil behavior set DisableDeleteNotify 0 and press Enter.
Restart the computer.
Optional: open "Defragment and Optimize Drives" and check that the SSD is set to be optimized weekly.
storage.trim.off.why: An SSD can't overwrite data in place; it has to erase blocks first. TRIM tells it which data Windows deleted, so it can erase those blocks in advance. Without TRIM it only finds out when it has to write there, which makes writes slower over time and causes extra wear.
memory.xmp.off.steps:
Restart the PC and press Delete or F2 repeatedly while it starts, to open the BIOS.
Find the XMP, EXPO or DOCP option (often on the first page, or under Ai Tweaker, OC or Extreme Tweaker).
Choose Profile 1 (or Enabled).
Save with F10 and restart.
If the PC won't start or crashes afterwards, turn the profile off again, or update the BIOS and try once more.
memory.xmp.off.why: Memory is sold with the speed of its XMP/EXPO profile, but without the profile it runs at the slower standard speed every PC can handle. The faster speed gives more FPS in games that lean on the processor, and helps integrated graphics a lot, because it uses the RAM as video memory. The profile is an overclock tested by the memory maker, so on a few PCs it isn't stable; that is why the last step is there.
memory.singlechannel.steps:
Look up in the motherboard manual which two slots to use for two modules (usually A2 and B2, the second and fourth from the processor).
Buy a second module that matches the one you have: same size and speed, ideally the same model. A kit of two new modules works too.
Shut down the PC, switch off the power supply and unplug it.
Insert the module into the right slot until both clips click.
Start the PC; the Memory page then shows dual channel.
memory.singlechannel.why: With one module the processor reaches memory over a single channel; with two modules in the right slots it uses two channels at once and gets twice the bandwidth. Games often gain 10 to 30 percent, and integrated graphics, which uses the RAM as video memory, can gain even more.
memory.xmp.stability.steps:
Restart the PC and press Delete or F2 while it starts, to open the BIOS.
Turn XMP/EXPO off (Disabled or Auto), save with F10 and restart.
Use the PC as usual for a few days.
If the crashes stopped: update the BIOS and turn XMP/EXPO back on, or choose one speed step lower than the profile.
If the crashes continue, the memory profile wasn't the cause: turn it back on and look at the other findings.
memory.xmp.stability.why: XMP/EXPO runs the memory faster than the processor is officially rated for. Whether that is stable depends on the processor's memory controller, the motherboard and the BIOS version, so a profile tested by the memory maker can still be borderline on one particular PC. Memory errors show up as random crashes and blue screens with changing error codes, which makes them easy to blame on something else.
gpu.display.igpu.steps:
Look at the back of the PC: the graphics card's outputs sit in a horizontal row lower down, in one of the expansion slots.
Move the monitor cable from the motherboard's port (next to the USB ports) to one of the graphics card's ports.
If the screen stays black, restart the PC.
If the picture still only comes from the motherboard, set the primary display to PCIe (or PEG) in the BIOS.
gpu.display.igpu.why: When the monitor is plugged into the motherboard, the picture comes from the processor's built-in graphics, or {0} has to send every frame through it. That costs FPS, adds delay, and can limit the refresh rate and G-Sync/FreeSync. Many people never notice, because games still start.
gpu.driver.old.steps:
Open the driver page of the card's maker: NVIDIA (nvidia.com/drivers or the NVIDIA app), AMD (amd.com/support or AMD Software), Intel (intel.com/support).
Download the newest driver for {0} and your Windows version.
Run the installer; choose a clean installation if it is offered.
Restart the computer.
gpu.driver.old.why: Graphics drivers get performance improvements for new games, fixes for crashes and black screens, and security fixes many times a year. A driver this old misses all of them, and newer games may refuse to start or show errors with it.
gpu.pcie.narrow.steps:
Shut down the PC, switch off the power supply and unplug it.
Check that the card sits in the top full-length slot (usually the one closest to the processor) and that the slot's latch has clicked.
If it is already there, look up in the motherboard manual whether an M.2 slot or the second long slot shares lanes with it, and move that drive or card if so.
If dust is visible in the slot, blow it out before reinserting the card.
gpu.pcie.narrow.why: The card talks to the processor over a number of lanes; x{1} is fewer than the x{2} it supports. On most cards x8 costs little, but x4 or x1 can cost noticeable FPS, especially on cards with little video memory, which often have to fetch data from RAM. A card that isn't fully seated can also drop lanes and later cause driver errors.
board.bios.old.steps:
Find the exact motherboard or laptop model on the Motherboard & System page.
Open that model's support page on the maker's website and download the newest BIOS.
Follow the maker's instructions; most boards update from a USB stick inside the BIOS (EZ Flash, M-Flash, Q-Flash).
Keep the PC switched on and plugged in until the update has finished.
Afterwards turn XMP/EXPO back on, because an update resets the BIOS settings.
board.bios.old.why: BIOS updates fix memory compatibility and stability problems, bring processor microcode fixes (some of them against crashes and chip wear), support newer processors and close security holes. An old BIOS is a common reason for freezes with newer memory or graphics cards. The one real risk is losing power during the update, which is why the PC must stay on.
cpu.ryzen.idle.steps:
Update the BIOS to the newest version first.
Restart the PC and press Delete or F2 while it starts, to open the BIOS.
Look for "Power Supply Idle Control" (often under Advanced → AMD CBS → CPU Common Options).
Set it to "Typical Current Idle", save with F10 and restart.
If you can't find the option, keep the BIOS defaults; the update alone often fixes it.
cpu.ryzen.idle.why: At very low load a Ryzen processor can drop into a deep sleep state where it draws almost no current. Some power supplies, often older ones, can't hold their voltages steady at such a tiny load, and the PC freezes or restarts while nobody is using it. "Typical Current Idle" keeps the current a little higher, which costs only a watt or two.
perf.rebar.off.steps:
Check that Windows starts in UEFI mode: press Windows + R, type msinfo32, and look for "BIOS mode: UEFI".
Restart the PC and press Delete or F2 while it starts, to open the BIOS.
Set CSM (Compatibility Support Module) to Disabled.
Turn on "Above 4G Decoding" and "Re-Size BAR Support" (often under Advanced → PCI Subsystem Settings).
Save with F10 and restart, then update the graphics driver.
perf.rebar.off.why: Without Resizable BAR the processor sees only a small window of the graphics card's memory at a time and keeps moving it around. With it, it sees all of the memory at once, so textures and other data reach the card faster. The gain is usually up to 10 percent, more in some games, and Intel Arc cards need it to perform well at all. Important: if msinfo32 says "Legacy", don't turn CSM off, or Windows won't start; the disk has to be converted to GPT first.

Restart the PC and press Delete or F2 repeatedly while it starts, to open the BIOS.
Find the XMP, EXPO or DOCP option (often on the first page, or under Ai Tweaker, OC or Extreme Tweaker).
Choose Profile 1 (or Enabled).
Save with F10 and restart.
If the PC won't start or crashes afterwards, turn the profile off again, or update the BIOS and try once more.

The profile is an overclock tested by the memory maker, so on a few PCs it isn't stable; that is why the last step is there.

Start the PC; the Memory page then shows dual channel.
