perf.mouse.accel.title: Mouse acceleration ("Enhance pointer precision") is on
perf.mouse.accel.detail: The pointer goes further when you move the mouse faster, so the same hand movement doesn't always turn the camera by the same amount.
perf.mouse.accel.fix: Turn off "Enhance pointer precision" in Settings → Bluetooth & devices → Mouse → Additional mouse settings → Pointer Options.
perf.mouse.accel.steps:
Open Settings (Windows + I) → Bluetooth & devices → Mouse.
Click "Additional mouse settings".
Open the Pointer Options tab.
Untick "Enhance pointer precision" and click OK.
If the pointer now feels slow on the desktop, raise the pointer speed or the mouse's DPI instead.
perf.mouse.accel.why: With acceleration, Windows stretches fast movements more than slow ones, so how far the pointer travels depends on how fast you move, not only how far. Your hand can't learn that, which makes aiming inconsistent. Games that read the mouse directly ignore it, but many older games, menus and launchers don't. On a laptop touchpad acceleration helps, so keep it if you mostly use the touchpad.
perf.windowed.off.title: "Optimizations for windowed games" is off
perf.windowed.off.detail: Games in a window or borderless window then show their frames the old way: with more delay, and without Auto HDR or G-Sync/FreeSync.
perf.windowed.off.fix: Turn it on in Settings → System → Display → Graphics → Advanced graphics settings.
perf.windowed.off.steps:
Open Settings (Windows + I) → System → Display → Graphics.
Click "Advanced graphics settings" (on older versions: "Change default graphics settings").
Turn on "Optimizations for windowed games".
Restart the game.
perf.windowed.off.why: Older DirectX 10 and 11 games in borderless mode let the desktop redraw every frame, which adds a frame of delay and blocks variable refresh rate and Auto HDR. This setting moves them to the newer way DirectX 12 games already use, so borderless plays like fullscreen. Recent Windows 11 versions turn it on by default; something turned it off on this PC.
perf.gpu.powersaving.title: {0}: set to run on the power-saving graphics
perf.gpu.powersaving.detail: Windows' graphics settings send these games to the integrated graphics instead of {1}.
perf.gpu.powersaving.fix: Set them to "High performance" (or "Let Windows decide") in Settings → System → Display → Graphics.
perf.gpu.powersaving.steps:
Open Settings (Windows + I) → System → Display → Graphics.
Find the game in the list of apps.
Click it and choose "High performance" (or "Let Windows decide").
Restart the game.
perf.gpu.powersaving.why: Integrated graphics shares the processor's power and the system memory and is many times slower than {1}. A game set to "Power saving" runs there however strong the graphics card is, which shows as very low FPS while the card sits idle. The setting is easy to change by accident, and some battery tools change it.
perf.x3d.driver.title: AMD's 3D V-Cache driver is missing ({0})
perf.x3d.driver.detail: Only one of the processor's two core dies has the extra cache. Without AMD's driver, games can run on the other one and lose much of the X3D advantage.
perf.x3d.driver.fix: Install the latest AMD Chipset Software from amd.com/support and restart the computer.
perf.x3d.driver.steps:
Open amd.com/support and look up your motherboard's chipset (for example X670 or B650) or your processor.
Download and run the newest AMD Chipset Software.
Restart the computer.
Make sure Xbox Game Bar is installed (Microsoft Store) and keep the Balanced power plan; the driver needs both.
Run CHC again: this tip disappears once the driver is there.
perf.x3d.driver.why: On the {0}, one core die has the large 3D V-Cache that games love, the other has higher clock speeds. AMD's driver uses Game Bar to recognise a game and parks the cores of the other die while you play, so the game stays on the cache die. Without it, Windows spreads the game over both dies, and frame rates can drop by 10 to 30 percent in games that need the cache.
perf.x3d.powerplan.title: The power plan "{1}" works against the {0}
perf.x3d.powerplan.detail: High and Ultimate Performance keep every core awake, so AMD's driver can't park the cores without the extra cache while you play.
perf.x3d.powerplan.fix: Switch back to the Balanced plan.
perf.x3d.powerplan.steps:
Press Windows + R, type control powercfg.cpl and press Enter.
Choose "Balanced" (open "Show additional plans" if you can't see it).
On Windows 11 you can also set Settings → System → Power → Power mode to "Best performance"; that keeps the Balanced plan.
Restart the game.
perf.x3d.powerplan.why: The {0} keeps games on its cache die by parking the cores of the other die while a game runs. The High and Ultimate Performance plans switch core parking off, so games can end up on the slower die for them. On this processor the Balanced plan costs no gaming performance.
gpu.display.resolution.title: Windows runs at {0} on a {1} display
gpu.display.resolution.detail: Everything is stretched to fill the screen, so text and the desktop look soft or blurry.
gpu.display.resolution.fix: Choose {1} (marked "Recommended") in Settings → System → Display, and use Scale to make things bigger.
gpu.display.resolution.steps:
Right-click the desktop and choose Display settings.
Under "Display resolution" choose {1} (marked "Recommended").
If text is now too small, raise "Scale" (for example to 125% or 150%) instead of lowering the resolution.
In games you can still pick a lower resolution, or better, turn on DLSS, FSR or XeSS.
gpu.display.resolution.why: A flat screen has a fixed number of pixels. At any other resolution the picture has to be stretched, and lines that should be one pixel wide smear across two. Windows' Scale setting makes text and icons bigger while every pixel stays sharp, so it is the right way to make things larger.
board.startup.many.title: {0} programs start with Windows
board.startup.many.detail: Among them: {1}. Each one makes start-up slower, and many keep running in the background.
board.startup.many.fix: Turn off the ones you don't need right away in Task Manager → Startup apps.
board.startup.many.steps:
Press Ctrl + Shift + Esc to open Task Manager.
Open "Startup apps" (the speedometer icon on the left).
Sort by "Startup impact".
Right-click programs you don't need the moment Windows starts (launchers, updaters, chat apps) and choose Disable.
Keep your antivirus and your audio, touchpad and graphics software, then restart to see the difference.
board.startup.many.why: Startup programs load while Windows is still starting, so they compete for the disk and processor and the desktop becomes usable later. Many then stay in the background, using memory, and sometimes processor time and network during games. Disabling only stops the automatic start: the program still works when you open it yourself.
perf.games.title: Your games
perf.games.detail: How each game runs on this PC, what holds it back and what to change.
perf.games.empty: Games show up here after about 10 minutes of fullscreen play.
perf.games.nofps: Frame rates are only recorded while CHC runs as administrator. Load and temperatures are recorded either way, so the advice here works without them, with less detail.
perf.games.off: The history is turned off, so CHC can't follow your games. You can turn it on in Settings.
perf.games.subtitle: {0} in the last 30 days · last played {1}
perf.games.chart: Average FPS and the slowest 1%, per day
game.limit.gpu.detail: At full load {0:0}% of the time
game.limit.unknown.detail: Needs the frame rate to tell
game.good.title: {0} runs well: about {1:0} FPS
game.good.detail: Nothing in the history holds it back.
game.fps.afterchange.title: {0} got slower after a change: {1:0} → {2:0} FPS
game.fps.afterchange.detail: The change: {3}, on {4}. The game ran at about {1:0} FPS in the two weeks before it and at {2:0} FPS since. A game patch or different maps can play a part, but a change that lines up like this is the first thing to check.
game.fps.afterchange.steps:
Open the Changes page and find the change.
Undo it if you can.
Play the game for at least half an hour as usual; CHC keeps recording.
If the FPS comes back, stay on the older version and try the next new one when it comes out.
game.fps.afterchange.why: The game, the PC and usually the settings are the same on both sides of the change, which makes this a fairer test than a benchmark from someone else's PC. Drivers and updates sometimes slow down one game by accident, and that gets fixed in a later version.
game.fps.drop.title: {0} runs slower than it used to: {1:0} → {2:0} FPS
game.fps.drop.detail: About {1:0} FPS earlier this month and {2:0} FPS in the last 7 days. No driver, update or BIOS change lines up with it.
game.fps.drop.fix: Check whether the game's settings changed or a game patch came out, then look at what runs in the background and at the temperatures.
game.fps.drop.steps:
Check the game's graphics settings; patches sometimes reset them.
Open Task Manager (Ctrl + Shift + Esc) while playing and sort by CPU to see what else is busy.
Compare the temperatures here with the History page: a dusty PC gets slower little by little.
If you play different maps or modes now, compare the same one again.
game.fps.drop.why: A game's frame rate depends on what is on screen, so small changes are normal. A lasting drop of more than a tenth usually has a cause: a patch, changed settings, a new background program, or more heat.
game.gpu.limited.title: The graphics card limits {0}
game.gpu.limited.detail: It was at full load {1:0}% of the {2} you played, so the game would run faster if the card could keep up.
game.gpu.lower.generic: Lower shadows, volumetric effects and ray tracing first, or turn on {0} in Quality mode.
game.gpu.limited.steps:
Open the game's graphics settings.
Lower one setting a step and check the FPS. Shadows, volumetric effects, reflections and ray tracing usually give the most back.
Turn on DLSS, FSR or XeSS in Quality mode if the game has it.
Keep textures high if the graphics card has the memory; they cost little FPS.
If you'd rather not choose, take the next lower preset.
game.gpu.limited.why: Every frame is waiting for the graphics card, while the processor could deliver more. So whatever makes the card's work lighter turns directly into FPS. Upscaling draws the picture at a lower resolution and rebuilds it sharply, which often gives a third more FPS or better with little visible loss.
game.cpu.limited.title: The processor holds {0} back
game.cpu.limited.detail: The game averaged {1:0} FPS on your {2} Hz monitor while the graphics card worked at only {3:0}%, so it kept waiting for the processor.
game.cpu.limited.fix: Lower what loads the processor: {4}. Textures, anti-aliasing and resolution can stay high or go higher; the graphics card has room.
game.cpu.limited.steps:
Close the programs you don't need while playing, browsers first.
In the game, lower the settings that load the processor: view distance, crowd density, physics and simulation.
Check the memory on the Memory page: XMP/EXPO on and two modules make a real difference here.
Keep the processor cool: it slows down near its temperature limit.
Raise the picture settings that only load the graphics card; it costs little FPS here.
game.cpu.limited.why: The processor prepares each frame before the graphics card draws it. When it can't keep up, the card sits idle and lowering the picture settings gains almost nothing. Many games lean on a few processor cores, so this happens even when the total processor load looks low.
game.capped.title: {0} stays at about {1:0} FPS
game.capped.detail: The graphics card has room ({2:0}% on average), so a frame limit or VSync in the game or the graphics driver is probably holding it there. Your monitor can show {3} Hz.
game.capped.fix: For smoother motion, raise or remove the limit in the game's settings or in the graphics driver.
game.capped.steps:
Open the game's display or graphics settings and look for "Frame rate limit", "Max FPS" or "VSync".
Set the limit to your monitor's refresh rate.
Check the graphics driver's control panel too (NVIDIA Control Panel or AMD Software), which can have its own limit.
Some games are locked to a fixed FPS and can't go higher; then there is nothing to change.
game.capped.why: A frame limit keeps the PC cooler and quieter, so it can be a good choice. But with a faster monitor and power to spare, it also holds motion back and adds a little input delay. The choice is yours; CHC only points out that the limit is there.
game.headroom.title: {0} runs faster than your monitor can show
game.headroom.detail: About {1:0} FPS on a {2} Hz monitor, with the graphics card at {3:0}%.
game.headroom.fix: Raise the picture settings, or limit the frame rate to {4} FPS so the PC runs cooler and quieter. In competitive games you can keep the high FPS: it lowers input delay a little.
game.headroom.steps:
For a better picture: raise textures, anti-aliasing and shadows in the game's settings until the FPS comes down near {2}.
For a cooler, quieter PC: set the game's frame limit to {4}.
For competitive play: leave it as it is.
game.headroom.why: A {2} Hz monitor shows {2} pictures a second, so the rest of the frames never appear whole. They still cost power, heat and fan noise. The one thing extra frames do give is a slightly fresher picture when you click, which matters mostly in competitive shooters.
game.gpu.room.title: {0} leaves the graphics card room
game.gpu.room.detail: The card averaged {1:0}% while you played. The processor or a frame limit is holding the game back; with the frame rate CHC can tell which.
game.gpu.room.fix: You can raise the picture settings without losing much. Run CHC as administrator to record the frame rate.
game.gpu.room.why: A graphics card well below full load is waiting for something else, so a sharper picture costs little. Which of the two it is waiting for shows in the frame rate, which Windows only lets administrators measure.
game.stutter.title: {0} has uneven frame times
game.stutter.detail: About {1:0} FPS on average, but the slowest 1% of frames run at only {2:0} FPS, which feels like stutter.
game.stutter.fix: Close background programs, limit the frame rate a little below what the PC reaches, and keep the graphics driver up to date.
game.stutter.steps:
Close browsers and other programs before playing.
Set a frame limit a little below your average FPS, in the game or the graphics driver.
Update the graphics driver.
Check that the game is on an SSD.
If it only happens in the first minutes of a session, the game is building its shader cache, and that passes.
game.stutter.why: The average hides what you feel: a few slow frames stand out however high the rest are. A frame limit gives the PC some slack, so every frame takes about the same time and motion looks smoother even at a lower average.
game.hot.gpu.title: {0} runs the graphics card hot (up to {1:0} °C)
game.hot.gpu.detail: Near their limit graphics cards lower their clocks to protect themselves, which costs FPS, and the fans get loud.
game.hot.gpu.fix: Clean the fans, improve the case airflow, or limit the game's frame rate.
game.hot.gpu.steps:
Shut the PC down and blow the dust out of the graphics card's fans and the case filters.
Check that the case fans pull air through the case and nothing blocks the vents.
Set a frame limit in the game: the card then has less to do.
If it stays hot, use a stronger fan curve in the card maker's tool or MSI Afterburner.
game.hot.gpu.why: Heat is the most common reason a PC gets slower over the years, and dust is its most common cause. A frame limit helps right away because a card that doesn't draw extra frames uses much less power, and that power is what turns into heat.
game.hot.cpu.title: {0} runs the processor hot (up to {1:0} °C)
game.hot.cpu.detail: Close to their limit processors lower their clocks, which costs FPS, usually as stutters.
game.hot.cpu.fix: Clean the cooler, check its mounting and the thermal paste, and improve the case airflow.
game.hot.cpu.steps:
Shut the PC down and clean the dust out of the cooler.
Check that the cooler's fan spins and that the cooler sits firmly.
Renew the thermal paste if the PC is a few years old.
Check the case fans' direction: air should go in at the front and out at the back or top.
game.hot.cpu.why: Some modern processors are designed to run close to their limit under full load, so a brief peak isn't damage. But if they stay there, they can't hold their top clocks, and games feel that first because they rely on a few fast cores.
perf.game.resolution.why: A monitor has a fixed number of pixels, so any other resolution gets stretched and looks soft, especially text and thin lines. Upscalers lower the resolution only for the 3D picture and rebuild it sharply, so they give the same speed-up with a cleaner image.
perf.game.windowed.why: In a window the desktop takes part in showing every frame, which adds delay and can block G-Sync/FreeSync. Fullscreen or borderless lets the game show its frames directly.
perf.game.vsync.why: VSync makes the game wait for the monitor, which stops tearing but adds input delay. A G-Sync or FreeSync monitor adapts to the game instead, so it prevents tearing without the wait; the limit a little below the maximum keeps the game inside the monitor's range.
perf.game.fpslimit.why: A limit below what the monitor can show holds motion back even when the PC has power to spare. A limit near the monitor's maximum still protects against wasted frames.
perf.game.renderscale.low.why: Below 100% the game draws fewer pixels and stretches them, which looks blurry. DLSS, FSR and XeSS also draw fewer pixels but rebuild the detail, so the same speed gain looks much sharper.
perf.game.renderscale.high.why: Above 100% the game draws more pixels than the screen has. It looks a bit sharper but the cost rises quickly: 150% means more than twice the pixels. On a card already at full load, this is the easiest large gain.
perf.game.upscaler.why: Upscaling draws the picture at a lower resolution and rebuilds it for the screen using earlier frames and motion data. In Quality mode the loss is hard to see, and the graphics card has far less to do, so FPS often rises by a third or more.
perf.game.reflex.why: When the graphics card is at full load, frames queue up before they are drawn, which you feel as delay between your mouse and the screen. Reflex keeps that queue empty, so the game responds faster, usually with no loss in FPS.
perf.game.gpuheavy.why: These settings load the graphics card more than the others and often change the picture less than their cost suggests. Lowering them one step usually gives more FPS than lowering everything a little.
perf.game.cpuheadroom.why: The graphics card is waiting for the processor, so picture settings cost little here. Settings that add objects and simulation load the processor, so those are the ones that give FPS.
perf.game.textures.why: Textures live in the graphics card's own memory. When it runs out, the game has to fetch them from the much slower system memory, which causes sudden stutters however fast the card is.
perf.game.lowhz.why: In exclusive fullscreen a game can switch the monitor to another refresh rate, and many pick a low one by default. The monitor then shows fewer pictures a second than it could, however many the PC produces.
perf.game.hdd.why: Games load textures and worlds from the disk while you play. A hard disk needs far longer to find the data than an SSD, so the game waits, which shows as stutter and very long loading times.
perf.ram.full.why: When the memory is full, Windows moves data to the disk, which is many times slower. If the game then needs that data back, it has to wait, and you feel a stutter.
perf.cpubound.why: The processor prepares each frame before the graphics card draws it. When it can't keep up, the card sits idle, and lowering picture settings gains almost nothing.
perf.gpubound.why: The graphics card is the part everything else waits for, which is normal in demanding games. It means the rest of the PC isn't holding it back, and that the settings decide your FPS.
perf.background.why: Whatever else runs competes with the game for processor time. A short burst at the wrong moment shows up as a stutter, even if the average looks small.
programs.page.subtitle: What each program uses of the processor, memory, disk and graphics card, in front or in the background.
programs.empty: This list fills up as you use the PC. Usage is saved every few minutes.
programs.off: The history is turned off, so CHC can't follow what programs use. You can turn it on in Settings.
programs.note: Processor and memory are averages while the program ran, as Task Manager counts them. Windows counts data sent over the network as data read and written too, so a download or upload also shows here.
program.background.cpu.title: {0} keeps the processor busy in the background
program.background.cpu.detail: It used {1:0.#}% of the whole processor on average over {2}, nearly all of that time behind other windows.
program.background.cpu.fix: Close it when you don't need it, or look in its settings for a way to make it work less. If you don't know the program, find out what installed it.
program.background.cpu.steps:
Check whether you need it running all the time.
Look in its settings for options like sync, scanning or indexing, and limit them.
If it starts with Windows and you don't need that, turn it off in Task Manager → Startup apps.
If you don't recognise it, right-click it in Task Manager, choose "Open file location" and look up the name. Run a virus scan if it still looks odd.
Update it: a program stuck at constant load is often a bug that is already fixed.
program.background.cpu.why: A program that does this much while nobody is looking takes processor time from whatever you are doing, and adds heat, noise and, on a laptop, battery drain. Most background programs should use almost nothing when they are idle, so a steady load usually means it is syncing, stuck, or doing work you didn't ask for.
program.windows.busy.title: {0} is busy ({1:0.#}% of the processor on average)
program.windows.busy.detail: This is part of Windows, so it isn't something to close. It often passes by itself after updates or a scan, but it shouldn't last for days.
program.windows.busy.fix: Restart the PC and let Windows Update finish. If it stays this busy, look the name up together with "high CPU": there is usually a known fix.
program.windows.busy.why: Parts of Windows work in the background after updates, while indexing files and during virus scans, and that load is normal for a while. Weeks of it usually point to something stuck, such as a failing update or a damaged search index.
program.gpu.background.title: {0} uses the graphics card in the background ({1:0.#}%)
program.gpu.background.detail: It keeps drawing with the graphics card even while it isn't the program in front.
program.gpu.background.fix: Close it when you don't need it, or turn off "hardware acceleration" and animated effects in its settings.
program.gpu.background.why: Whatever another program draws comes out of what a game can use, and it keeps the card from dropping to its quiet idle state. Overlays, animated wallpapers and browser tabs with video are the usual cases.
program.gpu.compute.title: {0} computes on the graphics card in the background ({1:0.#}%)
program.gpu.compute.detail: It isn't drawing anything: it uses the card for calculations, such as AI, video rendering or scientific work, while it isn't the program in front.
program.gpu.compute.fix: If you started this work yourself, all is well. If you don't recognise the program, find out what it is and run a virus scan.
program.gpu.compute.steps:
Check whether you started it: AI tools, video editors and 3D renderers do this on purpose.
If not, right-click it in Task Manager and choose "Open file location".
Look up the program's name.
Run a full virus scan if you still can't explain it.
program.gpu.compute.why: Hidden cryptocurrency miners work exactly like this, which is why it is worth a look when you can't explain it. There are many harmless reasons too, so this alone doesn't mean anything is wrong.
program.disk.writes.title: {0} writes about {1} a day
program.disk.writes.detail: That is a lot for a program in the background. Windows counts data sent over the network here too, so a backup or upload can be part of it.
program.disk.writes.fix: Check its settings for sync, logging or cache options, or move its data to another drive.
program.disk.writes.why: Steady writing keeps the disk busy, which other programs can feel, especially on a hard disk. SSDs are rated for a certain total amount of writing, so years of this can also use up their life sooner.
program.memory.pressure.title: Memory is often almost full ({0:0}% of the time)
program.memory.pressure.detail: Your PC has {2} of memory. The biggest users, on average: {1}.
program.memory.pressure.fix: Close what you don't need while working or gaming. If this is your normal way of using the PC, more memory would help.
program.memory.pressure.steps:
Close the programs above when you don't need them; in a browser, close tabs you aren't using.
Turn off programs that start with Windows but aren't needed: Task Manager → Startup apps.
Check the Memory page: if a slot is free, adding a module is usually a simple upgrade.
program.memory.pressure.why: When memory runs out, Windows moves data to the disk, which is far slower. Everything then feels sluggish, and games stutter. Unused memory is wasted, so high use is fine in itself; it is being near the limit most of the time that hurts.
game.ram.full.title: RAM was almost full while you played {0} ({1:0}%)
game.ram.full.detail: The game itself used about {2}. Next to it: {3}.
game.ram.full.fix: Close those programs before you play. If it still fills up, more memory helps this game.
game.ram.full.steps:
Close the programs named above before starting the game; tabs in a browser count too.
Check that the game is the only heavy program left in Task Manager (Ctrl + Shift + Esc).
Play as usual: CHC records the difference here.
If memory still fills up with little else running, think about adding memory.
game.ram.full.why: When memory is this full, Windows starts moving data to the disk, and the game has to wait when it needs that data back. You feel that as stutter even when the average FPS looks fine, and closing other programs is the easiest cure.
game.background.title: Other programs were busy while you played {0}
game.background.fix: Close what you don't need while playing. Turn off the overlays and hardware acceleration of the programs you keep open.
game.background.why: Each of these takes processor or graphics time away from the game, and a short burst at the wrong moment shows as a stutter even if the average looks small.
game.gpu.integrated.title: {0} runs on the integrated graphics ({1})
game.gpu.integrated.detail: Your PC also has {2}, which is much faster, but the game isn't using it.
game.gpu.integrated.fix: Set the game to "High performance" in Settings → System → Display → Graphics.
game.gpu.integrated.steps:
Open Settings (Windows + I) → System → Display → Graphics.
Find the game in the list; add its exe with "Browse" if it isn't there.
Choose "High performance" and save.
On a desktop, check that the monitor is plugged into the graphics card.
Restart the game.
game.gpu.integrated.why: Graphics built into the processor shares its power and uses system memory, so it is many times slower than a separate card. Laptops pick one for each program to save battery, and they sometimes pick the slow one for a game.
stability.sameapp.title: Most freezes and crashes came while {0} was in front
stability.sameapp.detail: {1} of the {2} that the history saw. Either this program itself is the problem, or it is the one that loads the PC enough to bring a hardware problem out.
stability.sameapp.fix: Update the program and the graphics driver. If it still happens, test the PC with something else that loads it just as hard.
stability.sameapp.steps:
Update the program, and for a game check its files (Steam: Properties → Installed Files → Verify).
Update the graphics driver.
Remove any overclock or undervolt while testing.
Run another heavy program or a stress test. If that crashes too, look at the hardware: power supply, temperatures, memory.
If only this program crashes, look for known problems with it, or lower its settings.
stability.sameapp.why: A pattern like this narrows the search a lot. If only one program brings the PC down, the problem is often in that program or the driver it uses. But heavy games are also what pushes a weak power supply or an unstable overclock over the edge, so the second test tells the two apart.
stability.underload.title: Freezes and crashes come under heavy load
stability.underload.detail: In {0} of the {1} that the history saw, the processor or graphics card was working hard right before.
stability.underload.fix: Check temperatures and the power supply, and remove any overclock or undervolt to test.
stability.underload.steps:
Remove any overclock or undervolt, including XMP/EXPO, for a while.
Check the temperatures on the History page for the time of the crash.
Check the Power page: is the power supply big enough, and are its power cables pushed in fully?
Update the graphics driver and the BIOS.
stability.underload.why: Heavy load is when the PC needs the most power and makes the most heat, so that is when a borderline power supply, too much heat or an unstable overclock shows up. Crashes that only come under load point away from software that runs all the time.
stability.atidle.title: Freezes and crashes come while the PC is doing almost nothing
stability.atidle.detail: In {0} of the {1} that the history saw, the processor and graphics card were nearly idle right before.
stability.atidle.fix: Look at power saving first: PCI Express power saving, deep processor sleep states and the BIOS version.
stability.atidle.steps:
Update the BIOS and the chipset driver.
Turn off PCI Express power saving (the findings on this page show how).
On AMD Ryzen, set "Power Supply Idle Control" to "Typical Current Idle" in the BIOS.
Do a memory test, because memory errors can also show up at any time.
stability.atidle.why: At idle the processor and other parts drop into deep power-saving states, and waking up from them is a delicate moment. Some hardware and drivers handle that badly, and some power supplies can't hold steady at very low load. Heat and overload are unlikely here, which narrows the search.
close.title: Keep recording in the background?
close.text: CHC only records temperatures, frame rates and program use while it runs. In the background it uses very little and waits next to the clock, where you can open it again.
close.remember: Don't ask again (you can change this in Settings)
settings.close.detail: Keep recording next to the clock, or exit CHC completely. While CHC is closed, the history has a gap.
devices.page.subtitle: What is connected to this PC, by cable or wirelessly, and what is wrong with it.
devices.empty: No devices found. Run a scan as administrator if this looks wrong.
device.usbport.title: USB problem: {0}
device.usbport.2: a device on this port failed to start
device.usbport.3: a device on this port stopped with a general failure
device.usbport.4: a device on this port draws too much current, so the port was switched off
device.usbport.5: a device on this port doesn't get enough power
device.usbport.6: the USB port doesn't have enough bandwidth for this device
device.usbport.fix: Unplug the device and plug it into a different USB port, on the back of the PC if you can, without a hub.
device.usbport.steps:
Unplug the device.
Plug it into a different port, preferably directly on the back of the PC.
If it is on a hub or a long cable, try without them; a powered hub helps devices that need much power.
Try the device on another PC: if it fails there too, the device or its cable is faulty.
If the port fails with every device, update the chipset driver and the BIOS.
device.usbport.why: Each USB port has limits on power and data. A faulty cable, a device that draws too much, or a hub with too much on it trips them, and Windows then switches the port off to protect it. Changing one thing at a time tells you whether it is the device, the cable or the port.
device.problem.title: {0} has a problem
device.problem.fix: Open Device Manager, right-click the device, choose "Update driver", or uninstall it and restart so that Windows sets it up again.
device.problem.steps:
Press Windows + X and choose Device Manager.
Find the device with the warning sign and double-click it.
Read what the General tab says.
On the Driver tab choose "Update driver", or install the newest one from the maker's site.
If that doesn't help, choose "Uninstall device" and restart the PC so that Windows sets it up again.
device.problem.why: Windows knows this device is there, but its driver couldn't start it or it reported a fault. Reinstalling clears a damaged setup, which is the most common cause. If the fault comes back with a fresh driver, the device itself may be failing.
device.drops.usb.title: {0} keeps dropping out ({1} times in {2} days)
device.drops.usb.detail: Windows saw it disconnect and come back within moments. If you didn't unplug it and don't use a switch or KVM, the connection is failing.
device.drops.usb.fix: Try another port on the back of the PC and another cable, and turn off USB power saving.
device.drops.usb.steps:
Plug it directly into a port on the back of the PC, not a hub or a front-panel port.
Try a different cable; a worn cable or plug is the most common cause.
In Device Manager, under "Universal Serial Bus controllers", open each "USB Root Hub" → Power Management, and untick "Allow the computer to turn off this device".
Turn off USB selective suspend in the power plan's advanced settings.
Update the chipset driver and the BIOS.
If it still drops out on another PC, the device is failing.
device.drops.usb.why: A USB device that drops for a moment loses everything in progress, which you feel as a frozen pointer, missed keys or a game losing its controller. Front panels and hubs add extra connections that can loosen, and Windows' power saving can switch ports off. Going through these one at a time usually finds the cause, and CHC keeps counting, so you'll see if it stops.
device.drops.wireless.title: {0} keeps losing its connection ({1} times in {2} days)
device.drops.wireless.detail: It disconnected and came back within seconds. Devices going to sleep take longer, so this looks like interference or a weak signal.
device.drops.wireless.fix: Move it closer to the PC, away from USB 3 ports and cables, and check its battery.
device.drops.wireless.steps:
Charge the device or replace its batteries.
Move it closer to the PC, with nothing metal in between.
Move USB 3 drives and cables away from the Bluetooth adapter: they disturb the same radio band.
If your Wi-Fi uses 2.4 GHz, try 5 GHz.
Update the Bluetooth driver.
Remove the device in Settings → Bluetooth & devices and pair it again.
device.drops.wireless.why: Bluetooth shares the 2.4 GHz band with Wi-Fi and is easily disturbed by USB 3, whose signals fall in the same range. Weak batteries also make the signal drop, often before a device warns about it.
device.slowusb.title: {0} runs at USB 2 speed
device.slowusb.detail: It can do USB 3 (5 Gbit/s or more), but is connected at 480 Mbit/s, about ten times slower.
device.slowusb.fix: Plug it into a USB 3 port (blue, or marked SS) with its original cable, without a USB 2 hub in between.
device.slowusb.steps:
Look for a USB port that is blue or marked SS, usually on the back of the PC.
Plug the device in there, directly.
Use the cable that came with it: many cables, especially for charging, only carry USB 2.
Check here again: the line under the device shows its speed.
If it stays at USB 2 on every port, update the chipset driver and check that USB 3 is on in the BIOS.
device.slowusb.why: A USB 3 connection needs extra wires in the port, the cable and any hub. If one of them lacks them, the device still works, but quietly at USB 2 speed, so large copies take many times longer and you get no warning.
device.battery.low.title: {0} is low on battery ({1}%)
device.battery.low.fix: Charge it or replace its batteries soon.
device.battery.low.why: Wireless devices often get less reliable as their battery runs down, with a weaker signal and more dropouts, sometimes before they warn you.
device.startfailed.title: {0} failed to start in the last {2} days (times: {1})
device.startfailed.detail: From Windows' log: it noticed the device, but couldn't get it running.
device.startfailed.fix: Try another USB port and the newest driver from the maker. If it works now, keep an eye on it.
device.startfailed.steps:
Unplug the device, and plug it into a different port, directly on the PC.
Install the newest driver from the maker's site.
In Device Manager, uninstall the device, then unplug it and plug it back in so that Windows sets it up again.
Update the chipset driver.
Try the device on another PC to see whether the device itself is at fault.
device.startfailed.why: When a device fails to start it may come back on the next try, so you only see it not working now and then. Windows keeps a note each time, which often gives the first hint of a poor connection or a driver problem.
device.wifi.drops.title: Wi-Fi lost its connection {0} times in {1} days
device.wifi.drops.detail: It came back within moments each time, so you didn't switch it off and the PC wasn't asleep. You feel this as calls freezing and downloads stopping.
device.wifi.drops.fix: Update the Wi-Fi driver, and turn off its power saving. If it continues, change the router's channel.
device.wifi.drops.steps:
Install the newest Wi-Fi driver from the PC's or the adapter's maker, not only from Windows Update.
In Device Manager, open the Wi-Fi adapter → Power Management, and untick "Allow the computer to turn off this device".
Move closer to the router, or use 5 GHz if you are on 2.4 GHz.
Change the router's Wi-Fi channel to one that is less crowded.
Check whether other devices drop at the same time: if they do, it is the router.
device.wifi.drops.why: Frequent short drops usually come from the driver, power saving, or a crowded channel, not from the internet line. CHC counts only the disconnects the connection came back from within moments, so a PC going to sleep isn't counted.
device.wifi.failed.title: Wi-Fi failed to connect {0} times in {1} days
device.wifi.failed.detail: Windows tried to join the network and couldn't.
device.wifi.failed.fix: Remove the saved network and join it again, and restart the router.
device.wifi.failed.steps:
Restart the router.
In Settings → Network & internet → Wi-Fi → Manage known networks, forget the network and join it again.
Update the Wi-Fi driver.
Check that the router's security setting (WPA2/WPA3) is one your adapter supports.
device.wifi.failed.why: Failed attempts usually come from a wrong saved password, a router that needs a restart, or a security mode the adapter doesn't handle. Forgetting the network clears a saved setup that has gone wrong.
device.wifi.weak.title: The Wi-Fi signal was weak {0}% of the time in the last {1} days
device.wifi.weak.detail: Below 40%, connections get slow and unstable.
device.wifi.weak.fix: Move the PC or the router so that fewer walls lie between them, or add a mesh point or a cable.
device.wifi.weak.steps:
Put the router up high in the open, not in a cupboard or behind a TV.
Count the walls between the router and the PC: each one costs a lot of signal.
Try 2.4 GHz if you are far away: it is slower, but it reaches further.
Add a mesh point or an extender halfway, or use a network cable if you can.
device.wifi.weak.why: With a weak signal the Wi-Fi falls back to lower speeds and has to send data again, so even a fast internet line feels slow. CHC notes how strong the signal is once a minute while it runs, and never the name of the network.

It marks them as "Non-CHC record", so you always know what CHC measured itself. Windows will ask for your permission, and nothing leaves this PC.

game.past.crashes.title: {0} crashed in the last {2} days ({1}×)
game.past.crashes.detail: Windows noted this. The crash came from {3}.
game.past.crashes.fix: Let the game's launcher check its files, and update the game. If the same file keeps coming up, search for its name together with the game's.
game.past.crashes.steps:
In the game's launcher, choose to verify or repair its files.
Install the game's latest update.
Update your graphics driver.
Remove any processor, memory or graphics overclock while you test.
Turn off overlays one at a time (Discord, Steam, GeForce, RivaTuner).
Search for the name of the crashing file together with the game's name: others have often found the cause.
game.past.crashes.why: When a program crashes, Windows notes which file it was in. A damaged game file or an overlay injected into the game are common causes that are quick to rule out.
game.past.crashes.rate.title: {0} crashes about once per {4:0.#} h of use ({1}× in the last {2} days)
game.past.crashes.rate.detail: Windows noted the crashes and the time played. Most crashes came from {3}.
game.past.crashes.rate.fix: Let the game's launcher check its files, and update the game and the graphics driver.
game.past.crashes.driver.title: {0} crashed in the graphics driver in the last {2} days ({1}×)
game.past.crashes.driver.detail: Windows noted this. The crash came from {3}, a part of the graphics driver.
game.past.crashes.driver.fix: Install a clean graphics driver, and remove any graphics overclock while you test.
game.past.crashes.driver.steps:
Install the newest driver from the maker's site, choosing a clean install; DDU removes the old one completely.
If the crashes started with a new driver, go back to the one before.
Remove any graphics card overclock or undervolt while you test.
Check the card's temperature in the Sensors page while you play.
Check that the card's power cables sit firmly.
game.past.crashes.driver.why: A crash inside the driver is usually the driver itself, the card being pushed too far, or an unstable power supply. It is less likely to be the game's fault when other games crash in the same file.
game.past.crashes.driver.rate.title: {0} crashes in the graphics driver, about once per {4:0.#} h of use
game.past.crashes.driver.rate.detail: Windows noted {1} crashes in the last {2} days. They come from {3}, a part of the graphics driver.
game.past.crashes.driver.rate.fix: Install a clean graphics driver, and remove any graphics overclock while you test.
game.past.crashes.after.title: {0} began to crash after a change: {1}
game.past.crashes.after.detail: It was played for hours without a crash before {2}. A change that lines up like this is the first thing to undo.
game.past.hangs.title: {0} stopped responding in the last {2} days ({1}×)
game.past.hangs.fix: Check the disk and memory pages of CHC, and let the game's launcher check its files.
game.past.lowmemory.title: Windows ran out of memory while {0} was on ({1}×)
game.past.lowmemory.detail: Windows noted this in the last {2} days, and named these as using the most: {3}.
game.past.lowmemory.fix: Close what you don't need before you play, and check that Windows may manage the page file itself.
game.past.lowmemory.steps:
Close browsers and other large programs before you play.
In System → About → Advanced system settings → Performance → Advanced → Virtual memory, choose to let Windows manage the page file.
Make sure the drive holding the page file has free space.
Lower the game's texture quality.
If this keeps happening, more memory will help.
game.past.lowmemory.why: When memory and page file both run out, Windows has to refuse programs what they ask for, and games crash or freeze. Windows notes this and names the biggest users at that moment.
game.past.alongside.title: These ran beside {0}: {1}
game.past.alongside.detail: Windows noted this during the hours you played. Each takes processor time away from the game.
game.past.alongside.fix: Close what you don't need while you play, or set it not to start with Windows.
game.past.alongside.why: Windows notes what every program used in each stretch of time, so this also covers the time before CHC was recording. Sync tools, updaters and browsers with many tabs are the usual ones.

Install the game's latest update.
Update your graphics driver.
Remove any processor, memory or graphics overclock while you test.
Turn off overlays one at a time (Discord, Steam, GeForce, RivaTuner).
Search for the name of the crashing file together with the game's name: others have often found the cause.
game.past.crashes.rate.why: When a program crashes, Windows notes which file it was in. A damaged game file or an overlay injected into the game are common causes that are quick to rule out.
game.past.crashes.driver.rate.steps:
Install the newest driver from the maker's site, choosing a clean install; DDU removes the old one completely.
If the crashes started with a new driver, go back to the one before.
Remove any graphics card overclock or undervolt while you test.
Check the card's temperature in the Sensors page while you play.
Check that the card's power cables sit firmly.
game.past.crashes.driver.rate.why: A crash inside the driver is usually the driver itself, the card being pushed too far, or an unstable power supply. It is less likely to be the game's fault when other games crash in the same file.
game.past.crashes.after.why: Drivers and updates change what a game runs on. When a game ran for hours without a crash and then begins to crash right after a change, that change comes first on the list of suspects.
game.past.hangs.why: A game that stops responding is often waiting for something slow: a disk that is failing or full, or memory that ran out.

welcome.title: Welcome to CHC
welcome.text: CHC checks how healthy your PC is, and tells you in plain words what's wrong and how to fix it.
welcome.point.plain.name: No technical knowledge needed
welcome.point.plain: Every problem comes with what it means and what to do, step by step.
welcome.point.private.name: What it finds stays on this PC
welcome.point.private: No account and no ads. To look for new drivers it asks their makers about your graphics card and chipset; nothing else about your PC is sent anywhere.
welcome.point.quick.name: This guide takes about a minute
welcome.point.quick: You can skip the tour, the settings, or both.
welcome.tour1.title: See how your PC is doing
welcome.tour1.text: CHC is already checking your PC. The results wait for you on these pages.
welcome.tour1.overview: A score out of 100, and what needs attention first.
welcome.tour1.parts.name: Processor, Memory, Storage, Graphics
welcome.tour1.parts: A page for each part: how it is doing, and all its details.
welcome.tour1.stability: Freezes, crashes and blue screens, and what most likely caused them.
welcome.tour1.fix.name: How to do it, and why
welcome.tour1.fix: Open this under a problem to see the steps that fix it, and why they help.
welcome.tour2.title: Find out what changed
welcome.tour2.text: A PC rarely gets worse overnight. These pages help you see when it began.
welcome.tour2.history: Temperatures, load and power over days and weeks.
welcome.tour2.changes: Drivers, updates and new hardware, next to when the problems started.
welcome.tour2.programs: What each program uses, in front and in the background.
welcome.tour2.lookback: When the PC was on and what ran, even from before CHC was installed.
welcome.tour3.title: Look closer when something feels off
welcome.tour3.text: Games, your connection and what's plugged in, plus a report to share.
welcome.tour3.games: FPS while you play, what holds your games back, and what to change.
welcome.tour3.network: Speed, delay and dropouts, when you start the test.
welcome.tour3.devices: What's plugged in, and a warning if a device has a driver or connection problem.
welcome.tour3.report: A PDF in one click, to keep or to show someone who can help.
welcome.settings1.title: Set it up your way
welcome.settings1.text: All of this is optional. The choices already made suit most people, and you can change them any time in Settings.
welcome.settings2.title: A few more choices
welcome.settings2.text: Also optional. If you're not sure, leave them as they are.
welcome.theme.why: "Use Windows setting" follows your PC's light and dark mode.
welcome.history.what: While CHC runs, it notes temperatures, load and the program in front.
welcome.history.why: So it can show when a problem began and what was going on then. It uses very little, and stays on this PC.
welcome.startup.what: CHC starts quietly next to the clock when you sign in.
welcome.startup.why: The history has a gap whenever CHC isn't running, so this catches problems whenever they happen. Windows asks for permission once.
welcome.close.what: Decides what the X button does.
welcome.close.why: "Keep recording" goes on next to the clock, using very little. "Exit CHC" stops it, which leaves a gap in the history.
welcome.admin.what: Restarts CHC with the rights Windows requires for CPU temperature, disk health and FPS in games.
welcome.admin.why: Without them CHC still works, with fewer details. Windows asks for permission when you finish this guide.
welcome.admin.tip: CHC restarts when you finish this guide.
welcome.notes.what: Windows notes which programs run. CHC can read that, keep it up to date, and marks it as "Non-CHC record".
welcome.notes.why: You see your games, crashes and two months of use right away, instead of waiting for CHC to collect them. Windows asks for permission, and nothing leaves this PC.
welcome.done.title: You're all set
welcome.done.text: CHC is checking your PC, and the results will be on the Overview page.
welcome.done.later: You can change any of this later in Settings, and find this guide there too.
